title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
任民望
同考試官教諭何　批　〔聖德大化最難名言是作不露上下本文體認親切可嘉〕
考試官學正蔡　批　〔善言君德者錄之〕
考試官學正周　批　〔非深沐聖人之化者不能作此〕
聖人之心純於仁而天下之心孚於仁大臣歸
功之意至矣甚矣仁道至大也聖人之心純矣
天下有不孚焉者乎皐陶因舜美其功而不敢
居故言此以歸之舜也若曰大帝德之罔愆不
===
惟其臨下之簡御衆之寬而用刑行賞之仁有
非刑賞之所能盡宜其及人者廣而入人者深
也何則大道無外以天下爲度故法不可獨任
焉曲成不遺以萬物爲體故仁不可勝用焉語
其心則天地生物之心語其德則天地好生之
德欲立欲達同其好惡而不違至公至神通乎
上下而無間賞足勸也惟其功而恩之所可伸
則雖僭有弗恤樂善之誠無少過焉刑足懲也
惟其罪而心之所尤切則雖縱有弗計不忍之
punctuated:
任民望

同考試官教諭何批〔聖德大化最難名言，是作不露上下本文，體認親切，可嘉。〕
考試官學正蔡批〔善言君德者，錄之。〕
考試官學正周批〔非深沐聖人之化者，不能作此。〕

聖人之心純於仁，而天下之心孚於仁，大臣歸功之意至矣。甚矣，仁道至大也！聖人之心純矣，天下有不孚焉者乎？皐陶因舜美其功而不敢居，故言此以歸之舜也。若曰：大帝德之罔愆，不惟其臨下之簡、御衆之寬，而用刑行賞之仁，有非刑賞之所能盡，宜其及人者廣，而入人者深也。何則？大道無外，以天下爲度，故法不可獨任焉；曲成不遺，以萬物爲體，故仁不可勝用焉。語其心，則天地生物之心；語其德，則天地好生之德。欲立欲達，同其好惡而不違；至公至神，通乎上下而無間。賞足勸也，惟其功，而恩之所可伸，則雖僭有弗恤，樂善之誠無少過焉；刑足懲也，惟其罪，而心之所尤切，則雖縱有弗計，不忍之
translation_en:
Ren Minwang

Associate Examiner He, Instructor, comments: 〔“Sagely virtue and its great transforming influence are exceedingly difficult to express in words. This composition does not explicitly invoke the surrounding text of the source passage; its understanding is intimate and precise, and deserves praise.”〕
Examiner Cai, School Instructor, comments: 〔“This speaks well of the ruler’s virtue; I select it.”〕
Examiner Zhou, School Instructor, comments: 〔“Only someone deeply imbued with the sage’s transforming influence could write this.”〕

The sage’s heart is pure in benevolence, and the hearts of all under Heaven respond trustingly to that benevolence: the great minister’s intention in attributing the achievement to his sovereign is expressed to the utmost. How vast indeed is the Way of benevolence! When the sage’s heart is pure, can anyone under Heaven fail to respond with trust? When Shun praised his achievements, Gao Yao dared not claim the credit, and therefore spoke these words to attribute it to Shun. It is as though he said: “Great Emperor, the faultlessness of your virtue lies not merely in your simplicity in dealing with subordinates and your generosity in governing the multitude. The benevolence with which you administer punishments and confer rewards extends beyond what punishments and rewards can fully express. It is fitting that its reach among people should be broad and its penetration of their hearts profound. Why is this? The great Way excludes nothing and takes all under Heaven as its measure; hence laws cannot be relied upon alone. It brings things to fulfillment in all their particularities, leaving nothing out, and takes the myriad things as its own body; hence benevolence is inexhaustible in its application. To speak of your heart is to speak of the heart with which Heaven and Earth engender living things; to speak of your virtue is to speak of the virtue with which Heaven and Earth cherish life. In desiring to establish yourself and attain fulfillment, you share the people’s likes and dislikes without departing from them. Utterly impartial and wondrously efficacious, your influence passes between those above and those below without obstruction. Rewards suffice to encourage: you attend to merit, yet wherever gracious favor can be extended, you do not worry even about excessive rewards; your sincerity in delighting in goodness contains not the slightest fault. Punishments suffice to deter: you attend to guilt, yet where your heart is especially moved, you do not reckon even the risk of undue leniency; your unwillingness to inflict suffering…”

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
□無自狹焉愛必其兼濟分不得而拘之太和
元氣之流行而充塞一何盛也惟民歸仁機固
相入耳澤必其下究勢不得而限之時雨江河
之膏潤而漸濡一何深也惟民有生理實相迎
耳至誠惻怛欲使人各協中而略無求備忿嫉
之私者純之至也一體相須能使民無不信而
咸有覆載生成之托者孚之極也是則君以民
之心為心民亦以君之心為心運天下於一心
通天下為一身合內外以成其仁斯舜德之罔
===
愆而民自不犯于刑也夫雖然陽舒陰慘仁育
義正可偏廢與天地之剥未嘗不復而扶陽抑
陰生生之意無時息焉帝王之治可知已虞廷
君臣更相嘆美曰無刑曰好生刑措則生遂矣
仁至則義盡矣一德同心猶想見當時氣象也
孟子有曰三代之得天下也以仁噫唐虞三代
之治必本於仁此其所以為盛與
皇建其有極斂時五福用敷錫厥庶民
王鋭
punctuated:
□無自狹焉。愛必其兼濟，分不得而拘之，太和元氣之流行而充塞，一何盛也！惟民歸仁，機固相入耳。澤必其下究，勢不得而限之，時雨江河之膏潤而漸濡，一何深也！惟民有生，理實相迎耳。至誠惻怛，欲使人各協中，而略無求備忿嫉之私者，純之至也；一體相須，能使民無不信，而咸有覆載生成之托者，孚之極也。是則君以民之心為心，民亦以君之心為心，運天下於一心，通天下為一身，合內外以成其仁，斯舜德之罔愆，而民自不犯于刑也。夫雖然，陽舒陰慘，仁育義正，可偏廢與？天地之剥，未嘗不復，而扶陽抑陰，生生之意無時息焉。帝王之治可知已。虞廷君臣更相嘆美，曰無刑，曰好生，刑措則生遂矣，仁至則義盡矣。一德同心，猶想見當時氣象也。孟子有曰：「三代之得天下也，以仁。」噫！唐虞三代之治必本於仁，此其所以為盛與？

皇建其有極，斂時五福，用敷錫厥庶民。
王鋭
translation_en:
…[illegible] does not narrow itself. His love necessarily extends aid to all; distinctions cannot constrain it. How abundantly the primordial vital energy of supreme harmony circulates and fills all things! The people turn toward benevolence because their inner impulses naturally accord with his. His beneficence necessarily reaches those below; differences in position cannot limit it. How deeply the nourishing moisture of timely rain and flowing rivers penetrates and soaks in! The people possess life, and its underlying principle truly responds to his. Utterly sincere and compassionate, he wishes everyone to accord with the mean, without the slightest selfish impulse to demand perfection or indulge anger and resentment: this is purity at its utmost. Mutually dependent as parts of one body, he inspires trust in all the people, so that all entrust themselves to his sheltering, sustaining, life-giving care: this is trust at its highest. Thus the ruler takes the people's heart as his heart, and the people likewise take the ruler's heart as theirs. He moves all under Heaven through one heart, unites all under Heaven as one body, and joins inner and outer to perfect his benevolence. Thus Shun's virtue was without fault, and the people of themselves committed no offenses punishable by law.

Yet yang brings ease and yin severity; benevolence nurtures and righteousness rectifies. Can either be neglected? In Heaven and Earth, stripping away is invariably followed by return; in supporting yang and restraining yin, the intention to generate life never ceases. From this we may understand the government of emperors and kings. At the court of Shun, ruler and ministers praised one another, speaking of doing away with punishment and of cherishing life. When punishments are set aside, life attains fulfillment; when benevolence reaches its height, righteousness is fully realized. United in virtue and of one heart, they still allow us to envision the spirit of that age. Mencius said: “The Three Dynasties gained all under Heaven through benevolence.” Ah! The government of Yao, Shun, and the Three Dynasties necessarily rested upon benevolence. Was this not why it flourished?

The sovereign establishes the supreme standard, gathers these five blessings, and thereby bestows them broadly upon his common people.
Wang Rui

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭何　批　〔君民之福並受本同一理惟子〕
能言之宜錄以式
考試官學正蔡　批　〔講斂福錫民處冲淡有味可錄〕
考試官學正周　批　〔發明題意殆盡〕
盡君道而得天以及民君子衍皇極之疇也甚
矣君身萬化之原也君道盡則爲法於天下矣
福之得於天而及於民也宜哉箕子演疇以告
武王見極之不可不建也如此且神禹以皇極
之疇第中五之數何哉數有奇偶而五居陰陽
===
之中疇有常變而皇極乃經權之主君人者誠
能取象於數效法於疇以身有常尊而表正之
責專道有定矩而統會之功大彝倫之體原於
天天下之公理也以先得之則易簡成位而心
極於是乎存焉彝倫之用備於人天下之大經
也以經綸之則中正爲觀而人極於是乎立焉
夫皇極之建雖自盡其道而無心於福之隆也
然天人之際甚微而感通之機無間心和則氣
無不和也氣和則形無不和也體信達順理之

考試官學正蔡　批：〔講斂福錫民處，冲淡有味，可錄。〕

盡君道而得天以及民，君子衍皇極之疇也。甚矣，君身萬化之原也！君道盡，則爲法於天下矣；福之得於天而及於民也，宜哉！箕子演疇以告武王，見極之不可不建也如此。且神禹以皇極之疇第中五之數，何哉？數有奇偶，而五居陰陽之中；疇有常變，而皇極乃經權之主。君人者誠能取象於數，效法於疇，以身有常尊，而表正之責專；道有定矩，而統會之功大。彝倫之體原於天，天下之公理也。以先得之，則易簡成位，而心極於是乎存焉。彝倫之用備於人，天下之大經也。以經綸之，則中正爲觀，而人極於是乎立焉。夫皇極之建，雖自盡其道而無心於福之隆也，然天人之際甚微，而感通之機無間。心和則氣無不和也，氣和則形無不和也。體信達順，理之
translation_en:
Associate Examiner He, Instructor, comments: 〔“The ruler and the people alike receive blessings: this rests on one and the same principle. You alone〕have been able to articulate it. This should be included as a model.”
Examiner Cai, Instructor, comments: 〔“The discussion of gathering blessings and bestowing them upon the people is restrained yet rich in meaning. Worth including.”〕
Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: 〔“This elucidates the meaning of the topic almost exhaustively.”〕
By fulfilling the ruler’s Way, one gains Heaven’s favor and extends it to the people: thus does the gentleman expound the category of the August Ultimate (huangji). How profoundly the ruler’s own person is the source of all transformation! When the ruler’s Way is fulfilled, he becomes a model for all under Heaven. How fitting, then, that blessings received from Heaven should reach the people! When Jizi expounded the categories to instruct King Wu, this was how he showed that the Ultimate must be established. Moreover, why did the divine Yu place the category of the August Ultimate in the central, fifth position? Numbers are odd or even, and five occupies the center between yin and yang; the categories encompass constancy and change, and the August Ultimate governs both abiding standards and discretionary judgment.
If the ruler of men can truly draw his pattern from the numbers and take the categories as his model, then, because his person holds enduring preeminence, the responsibility for setting others right through his example rests upon him alone; because the Way has a fixed standard, his achievement in unifying and bringing all together is great. The substance of the constant moral relationships originates in Heaven and constitutes the universal principle of all under Heaven. By apprehending it before others, he establishes his position through ease and simplicity, and thus the ultimate standard of the mind is preserved. The functioning of the constant moral relationships is fully realized among human beings and constitutes the great guiding norm of all under Heaven. By ordering it, he makes centrality and uprightness an example for others to behold, and thus the ultimate standard for humanity is established.
Although establishing the August Ultimate means fulfilling one’s own Way without deliberately seeking an abundance of blessings, the connection between Heaven and humanity is exceedingly subtle, and the workings of their mutual resonance admit no interruption. When the mind is harmonious, the vital force is harmonious in every respect; when the vital force is harmonious, physical form is harmonious in every respect. title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
不可誣者耳斂以五福則六極所當避者庶幾
其必免矣雖無心於福而不能不有心於民也
故君民之勢雖隔而相須之義實殷盡性以盡
人之性也立命以立人之命也作善降祥分之
所吝足者耳錫之庶民則有位而爲臣者亦在
所不遺矣吁極建而福自集福以極至皇非有
求於天也極建而民自化福與化俱天非有私
於民也天人應若影響君民義同休戚皆係於
極極其可以不建哉夫皇極建則彝倫敘而治
===
法無餘蘊矣然即繼之以斂福而錫民者見箕
子知道之深焉舜以聖人之德祿位名壽各臻
其極而當時之民亦風動以治猶齊政命官分
州考績兢業勤民天生聖人豈偶然之故哉皇
極一疇守常制變實統生成而造就臣民又爲
敷言以興起之何其至也孔子論德以北辰而
述六經敎萬世蓋深有合乎皇極之義矣謂之
不得其常可乎彼作五行傳以附會於天人之
徵應者其於聖賢之道何如也故曰箕子之言
punctuated: 不可誣者耳。斂以五福，則六極所當避者，庶幾其必免矣。雖無心於福，而不能不有心於民也。故君民之勢雖隔，而相須之義實殷。盡性以盡人之性也，立命以立人之命也。作善降祥，分之所吝足者耳。錫之庶民，則有位而爲臣者亦在所不遺矣。吁！極建而福自集，福以極至，皇非有求於天也；極建而民自化，福與化俱，天非有私於民也。天人應若影響，君民義同休戚，皆係於極，極其可以不建哉？夫皇極建，則彝倫敘，而治法無餘蘊矣。然即繼之以斂福而錫民者，見箕子知道之深焉。舜以聖人之德，祿位名壽各臻其極，而當時之民亦風動以治，猶齊政命官，分州考績，兢業勤民。天生聖人，豈偶然之故哉？皇極一疇，守常制變，實統生成而造就臣民，又爲敷言以興起之，何其至也！孔子論德以北辰，而述六經敎萬世，蓋深有合乎皇極之義矣。謂之不得其常，可乎？彼作《五行傳》以附會於天人之徵應者，其於聖賢之道何如也？故曰：「箕子之言
translation_en:
…is simply a principle that cannot be gainsaid. By gathering the five blessings, one may hope surely to escape the six extremities of misfortune that ought to be avoided. Though the ruler has no thought of blessings for himself, he cannot but concern himself with the people. Thus, although ruler and people are separated by their positions, their mutual dependence carries profound obligations. He fully realizes his own nature so as to enable others to realize theirs; he establishes his own allotted destiny so as to enable others to establish theirs. Doing good brings down auspicious blessings; the wording concerning their allotted share is unclear [?]. When these blessings are bestowed upon the common people, those who hold office as ministers are likewise not left out.

Ah! Once the standard is established, blessings gather of themselves. Blessings arrive through the standard; the sovereign has sought nothing from Heaven. Once the standard is established, the people are transformed of themselves. Blessings accompany this transformation; Heaven shows no partiality toward the people. Heaven and humanity respond to one another like shadow and echo; ruler and people are bound to share prosperity and adversity. All depends upon the standard. How, then, could it be left unestablished? Once the August Standard is established, the constant human relationships fall into order, and the methods of government have nothing left unexpressed. Yet the immediately following injunction to gather blessings and bestow them upon the people reveals how deeply Jizi understood the Way.

Through his sagely virtue, Shun attained the utmost in emolument, rank, renown, and longevity, while the people of his time responded to his influence as to the wind and became well governed. Even so, he ordered governmental affairs, appointed officials, divided the land into provinces, and assessed official performance, remaining vigilant and diligent in caring for the people. Could Heaven’s production of a sage have been merely accidental? The single category of the August Standard preserves the constant and governs change. It truly brings generation and nurture under its comprehensive direction, forming ministers and people; moreover, its teachings are expounded to rouse them. How consummate it is!

Confucius invoked the North Star when discussing virtue, and transmitted the Six Classics to teach ten thousand generations. This accords profoundly with the meaning of the August Standard. Can one say that he failed to grasp its constant principle? As for those who composed the Commentary on the Five Phases, forcing correspondences between Heaven and humanity into a scheme of signs and responses, how do they stand in relation to the Way of the sages and worthies? title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
爲傳道也
詩
天子命我城彼朔方赫赫南仲玁狁于襄
路王道
同考試官敎諭彭　批　〔以兵家成說敷演最爲親切且歸重王命辭婉意達誠可以鼓三軍而勵今將矣錄之以冠多士〕
同考試官敎諭翟　批　〔通篇皆見忠勇氣節讀之足以立頑起懦宜錄於式〕
考試官學正蔡　批　〔詞語雄健〕
===
考試官學正周　批　〔氣魄高邁〕
大將令衆以受命之重而因成靖遠之功焉甚
矣王道貴謀而賤戰也大將受命備邊而遠人
以服其得禦夷之道也乎此勞還帥之詩至此
則南仲傳君命以令軍衆也其意以爲帝王之
兵固出於萬全神武之威亢在於不殺今者以
玁狁之故方擇夫分閫之司而渙汗之頒自塵
於戒行之日鬭天王固嘗親命我矣其所以命
我者夫豈以攻討爲計哉蓋欲擇要害以扼其
punctuated:
爲傳道也。
詩
「天子命我，城彼朔方。赫赫南仲，玁狁于襄。」
路王道

大將令衆以受命之重，而因成靖遠之功焉。甚矣，王道貴謀而賤戰也！大將受命備邊，而遠人以服，其得禦夷之道也乎！此勞還帥之詩，至此則南仲傳君命以令軍衆也。其意以爲：帝王之兵，固出於萬全；神武之威，亢在於不殺。今者以玁狁之故，方擇夫分閫之司，而渙汗之頒，自塵於戒行之日。鬭天王固嘗親命我矣。其所以命我者，夫豈以攻討爲計哉？蓋欲擇要害以扼其
translation_en:
…was for transmitting the Way.

Book of Odes

“The Son of Heaven commanded me to fortify that northern region. Resplendent was Nan Zhong: the Xianyun were driven off.”

Lu Wangdao

Associate Examiner Peng, Instructor, comments: 〔The exposition draws upon established military teachings with particular aptness, while placing the emphasis on the king’s command. Its language is graceful and its meaning clearly conveyed. It could truly hearten the armies and spur today’s generals to action. We include it to head the candidates’ essays.〕

Associate Examiner Zhai, Instructor, comments: 〔Loyalty, courage, and moral resolve appear throughout. Reading it is enough to inspire the obdurate and rouse the timid. It should be included as a model.〕

Examiner Cai, School Instructor, comments: 〔The language is vigorous and forceful.〕

Examiner Zhou, School Instructor, comments: 〔Its spirit is lofty and far-reaching.〕

The great general commands his troops by impressing upon them the weight of the commission he has received, and thereby accomplishes the pacification of distant regions. How profoundly the kingly Way prizes planning and holds warfare cheap! The great general receives orders to defend the frontier, and the peoples of distant regions submit: has he not grasped the proper way to ward off the barbarians? This ode honors a commander returning from service. At this point, Nan Zhong conveys his ruler’s command to give orders to the troops. His meaning is this: the military undertakings of emperors and kings assuredly proceed from plans that ensure complete success; the awe of their divine martial power lies above all [?] in not killing. Now, because of the Xianyun, an officer was being selected to exercise independent military command, and the imperial proclamation reached my unworthy self [?] on the day preparations were made to depart. [?] The heavenly king had indeed personally given me his command. In commanding me, could he possibly have intended a campaign of assault and punishment? Rather, he wished me to select a strategic point so as to seize their…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
吭而荆方之地則宜有備禦焉者也于此城之
以明先王荒服之制將以我之不可勝制敵之
可勝而几此禦戎上策天子其親授矣敢不敬
承也哉據險阻以執其樞而干城之寄則所當
專任焉者也我其司之以峻外夷出入之防蓋
不恃其不來恃吾有以待之而臣此籌邊大略
王言其面命矣敢不祗若也哉夫是天子之命
將也固不以攻戰爲能而大將之制夷也亦豈
必戰而後克吾見此南仲也以有制之兵其紀
===
律夙嚴以必勝之將其威名素著何赫赫如之
故夫風聲所至蓋有不戰而屈人之兵者蠢爾
群醜莫不憚中國之有人而桀驁不臣之心已
潛消默奪之矣夫何嘗假兵車之力而必以善
戰爲能也乎威名所加蓋有先聲而奪人之氣
者奄彼遐荒罔不服王猶之允塞而畏威懷德
之念已感動興起之矣又何有肆憑陵之勢而
勤我孔棘之慮也乎夫君命將而得備禦之道
於此見內修之具也臣受命而布服遠之威於
punctuated: 吭，而荆方之地則宜有備禦焉者也。于此城之，以明先王荒服之制，將以我之不可勝制敵之可勝，而几此禦戎上策，天子其親授矣，敢不敬承也哉？據險阻以執其樞，而干城之寄則所當專任焉者也。我其司之，以峻外夷出入之防，蓋不恃其不來，恃吾有以待之，而臣此籌邊大略，王言其面命矣，敢不祗若也哉？夫是天子之命將也，固不以攻戰爲能；而大將之制夷也，亦豈必戰而後克？吾見此南仲也，以有制之兵，其紀律夙嚴；以必勝之將，其威名素著。何赫赫如之！故夫風聲所至，蓋有不戰而屈人之兵者。蠢爾群醜，莫不憚中國之有人，而桀驁不臣之心已潛消默奪之矣。夫何嘗假兵車之力，而必以善戰爲能也乎？威名所加，蓋有先聲而奪人之氣者。奄彼遐荒，罔不服王猶之允塞，而畏威懷德之念已感動興起之矣。又何有肆憑陵之勢，而勤我孔棘之慮也乎？夫君命將而得備禦之道，於此見內修之具也；臣受命而布服遠之威，於
translation_en:
…throat; and the territory of Jingfang 荆方 [?] is a place where defensive preparations should be made. Build fortifications here to make manifest the former kings’ arrangements for the outermost submission zone. By making ourselves invincible, we shall exploit the enemy’s vulnerability. This supreme strategy for warding off the Rong [?] has been personally imparted by the Son of Heaven. Dare we fail to receive it reverently? Occupy difficult terrain to hold the strategic pivot: the responsibility of serving as shield and rampart is one that the commander must assume exclusively. Let us take charge of it, strictly guarding against the passage of foreign peoples. We rely not on their failing to come, but on our having the means to meet them. This broad strategy for managing the frontier [?] has been conveyed face to face in the king’s own command. Dare we fail to obey respectfully?

Thus, when the Son of Heaven commissions a commander, he certainly does not regard offensive warfare as the measure of ability. And when a great commander brings foreign peoples under control, must he fight before he can prevail? We see that Nan Zhong 南仲 commands troops governed by established regulations, whose discipline has long been strict. As a commander certain of victory, his awe-inspiring reputation has long been renowned. How splendid he is! Wherever word of him reaches, there are indeed enemy armies subdued without battle. Those swarming bands of villains all fear that the central realm has capable men; their unruly refusal to submit has already been quietly dissolved and imperceptibly overcome. When has he ever needed to borrow the strength of war chariots or insist that prowess in battle alone constitutes ability?

Wherever his formidable reputation extends, its advance report is enough to rob others of their courage. Throughout those distant wilds, none fails to acknowledge that the king’s plans are truly comprehensive; thoughts of fearing his might and cherishing his virtue have already been stirred and awakened. How, then, could they unleash their aggressive power and burden us with pressing anxieties? When the ruler commissions a commander and grasps the proper way to prepare defenses, we see here the provisions for strengthening internal government. When the minister receives his commission and spreads the might that brings distant peoples into submission, here…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
此見外攘之功也周王之善將將衛代□□
兵不亦兩有足徵也哉抑觀夷狄之患自古有
之而所恃以無恐者顧我之自治何如耳孟子
有曰天時不如地利地利不如人和誠能設險
以守利而又修德以致和則遠人不足願矣何
外患之足慮哉故朱子曰其備不在邊境而在
朝廷其本不在威嚴而在德業斯言得之矣
右享之
儀式刑文王之典日靖四方伊嘏文王既
張世威
同考試官教諭彭　批〔法祖安民形容殆盡可謂善言〕
詩者
===
同考試官教諭崔　批〔語意冲雅仁孝之意藹然是用〕
錄出瑩
考試官學正蔡　批〔能體祭義之作〕
考試官學正周　批〔深得立言之旨〕
周人宗祀必言其法祖安民而決聖神之享也
蓋君德莫大於法祖也法祖以安民而神歆其
punctuated:
此見外攘之功也。周王之善將將，衛代□□兵，不亦兩有足徵也哉？抑觀夷狄之患，自古有之，而所恃以無恐者，顧我之自治何如耳。孟子有曰：「天時不如地利，地利不如人和。」誠能設險以守利，而又修德以致和，則遠人不足願矣，何外患之足慮哉？故朱子曰：「其備不在邊境而在朝廷，其本不在威嚴而在德業。」斯言得之矣。
右享之。
儀式刑文王之典，日靖四方。伊嘏文王，既。
張世威
同考試官教諭彭　批〔法祖安民，形容殆盡，可謂善言〕詩者。
同考試官教諭崔　批〔語意冲雅，仁孝之意藹然，是用〕錄出瑩。
考試官學正蔡　批〔能體祭義之作。〕
考試官學正周　批〔深得立言之旨。〕
周人宗祀，必言其法祖安民，而決聖神之享也。蓋君德莫大於法祖也，法祖以安民，而神歆其
translation_en:
…here we see the achievement of repelling external threats. The Zhou king’s skill in commanding his commanders, and Wei’s handling of troops [?—the transcription reads 衛代□□兵]: do not both furnish ample evidence? Yet troubles caused by the Yi and Di have existed since antiquity. What enables us to face them without fear depends simply on how well we govern ourselves. Mencius said: “Favorable timing is less important than advantageous terrain; advantageous terrain is less important than harmony among people.” If we can indeed establish defenses at strategic positions to preserve our advantage, and cultivate virtue to bring about harmony, there will be no need to covet the allegiance of distant peoples. What cause, then, is there to worry about external threats? Thus Master Zhu said: “Preparedness lies not at the frontier but at court; its foundation lies not in imposing authority but in virtuous deeds.” These words grasp the matter rightly.
“He assists and accepts the offering.” [An isolated fragment in the transcription.]
“Take King Wen’s statutes as your pattern, daily bringing peace to the four quarters. Ah, great King Wen, already…” [The quoted examination topic breaks off here in the transcription.]
Zhang Shiwei.
Associate Examiner Peng, Instructor, comments: “The description of following the ancestors and bringing peace to the people is almost exhaustive. He may be called one who speaks well about the Odes.”
Associate Examiner Cui, Instructor, comments: “The language and meaning are restrained and elegant; a spirit of benevolence and filial devotion is abundantly evident. For this reason it is…” The following characters, 錄出瑩, appear to refer to selection for inclusion, but are doubtful [?].
Examiner Cai, Director of Studies, comments: “A composition that embodies the meaning of sacrifice.”
Examiner Zhou, Director of Studies, comments: “It profoundly grasps the purpose underlying these words.”
In their ancestral sacrifices, the people of Zhou invariably spoke of following their ancestors and bringing peace to the people, thereby affirming that the sage spirit would accept their offerings. For no virtue of a ruler is greater than following his ancestors. By following his ancestors he brings peace to the people, and the spirit takes delight in his…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
德矣夫焉有不享其祀者哉此宗祀文王於明
堂以配上帝之樂歌至此謂夫備物以祀天吾
固不敢必其享與否也而其祀文王者則有可
必焉何以知其然葢懿典在前王固將望子孫
以駿惠而莫爲於後則前王之志拂矣聖德在
當世咸足以潤澤乎生民而世德不求則民生
之命戚矣今也仰丕顯之謨以銳作求之志而
凡吾之所以爲綏衆寧民之術者咸奉成憲以
周旋以緝熙之敬而勤率由之功於凡我之所
===
以爲又世康國之仁者皆守故典以勿替故今
天下之民各得其所而繼世之後無間於先典
法而民亦安矣夫然一氣相爲流通而精神之
運用不窮一德相爲後先而吾心之感格有素
則此能錫福之文王豈不享我之祀乎吾知嘉
嗣續之得人而典章賴以不墜則怨恫黜而思
成綏用綸之餘爾乎陟降之在日也慶成法之
可久而耿光用以不磨則降監昭而繁祉介牛
羊之右儼然聖祖之居歆也是文祖非私諸我
punctuated: 德矣，夫焉有不享其祀者哉？此宗祀文王於明堂以配上帝之樂歌，至此謂夫備物以祀天，吾固不敢必其享與否也；而其祀文王者，則有可必焉。何以知其然？葢懿典在前，王固將望子孫以駿惠，而莫爲於後，則前王之志拂矣；聖德在當世，咸足以潤澤乎生民，而世德不求，則民生之命戚矣。今也仰丕顯之謨，以銳作求之志，而凡吾之所以爲綏衆寧民之術者，咸奉成憲以周旋；以緝熙之敬，而勤率由之功，於凡我之所以爲又世康國之仁者，皆守故典以勿替。故今天下之民各得其所，而繼世之後無間於先典，法而民亦安矣。夫然，一氣相爲流通，而精神之運用不窮；一德相爲後先，而吾心之感格有素。則此能錫福之文王，豈不享我之祀乎？吾知嘉嗣續之得人，而典章賴以不墜，則怨恫黜而思成綏，用綸之餘爾乎陟降之在日也；慶成法之可久，而耿光用以不磨，則降監昭而繁祉介，牛羊之右，儼然聖祖之居歆也。是文祖非私諸我
translation_en:
…virtue, and how could the spirits fail to accept his sacrifice? This is the ritual song for honoring Wen Wang in the Hall of Enlightenment as the associate of the Lord on High. At this point it declares: “When I prepare offerings to sacrifice to Heaven, I certainly dare not presume whether they will be accepted. But concerning the sacrifice to Wen Wang, acceptance can be assured.” How do we know this? The excellent institutions stand before us, and the king surely expected his descendants to follow them faithfully. If those who come after accomplish nothing, the former king’s intentions are thwarted. Sagely virtue in its own age amply nourishes the people; but if the virtue handed down through the generations is not pursued, the people’s lot becomes grievous.

Now, looking up to those illustrious plans, we sharpen our resolve to carry them forward. In all our methods for pacifying the multitude and bringing peace to the people, we act in accordance with established statutes. With reverence that grows ever brighter, we diligently follow the inherited ways. In all our benevolent measures for aiding the age [?] and bringing tranquility to the state, we uphold the ancient institutions without allowing them to lapse. Thus the people throughout the realm now each find their proper place, and succeeding generations do not depart from the earlier institutions. The ancestors are emulated, and the people too are at peace.

In this way, a single vital force circulates between us, and the workings of spiritual vitality are inexhaustible. A single virtue links those who came before with those who follow, and my heart has long been prepared to move and reach the spirits. How, then, could Wen Wang, who can bestow blessings, fail to accept my sacrifice? I know that he rejoices that worthy successors have been found, through whom the institutions are preserved from decline. Resentment and suffering are banished, and the ancestral presence invoked by thought brings repose; the ensuing phrase concerning divine ordering and daily ascent and descent is doubtful [?]. He rejoices that the established laws can endure and that his brilliant glory thereby remains undimmed. His watchful gaze from above is manifest, and abundant blessings are bestowed. Beside the sacrificial oxen and sheep, the august ancestor seems solemnly present, accepting the offerings. This does not mean that the illustrious ancestor shows partiality toward us…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
也祀不以物而以志則感召之易孚我非有求
於文祖也神無常享而享于誠信來假之有本
其享我也不有以知其必然也哉噫是可謂能
盡理幽之義者矣吾嘗觀於周人明堂之祀將
享一詩不獨可以昭祀典也而敬天之誠法祖
之義勤民之惠胥得之矣是故畏威敬天也式
典法祖也靖四方勤民也君道孰有大於此三
事者乎周人一舉而兼盡之周之德可謂至德
也已矣噫此周家所以有道之長而凡有天下
===
國家者尚其鑒之
春秋
春王正月公會齊侯宋公陳侯衛侯鄭伯
許男曹伯侵蔡蔡潰遂伐楚次于陘
楚屈完來盟于師盟于召陵〔僖公四年〕
馬出圖
考試官學正蔡　批〔序齊桓伐楚之績處深合傳意〕
是邃於經學者
考試官學正周　批〔謹嚴〕
punctuated:
也。祀不以物而以志，則感召之易孚。我非有求於文祖也，神無常享，而享于誠信，來假之有本。其享我也，不有以知其必然也哉？噫！是可謂能盡理幽之義者矣。吾嘗觀於周人明堂之祀，《將享》一詩，不獨可以昭祀典也，而敬天之誠、法祖之義、勤民之惠，胥得之矣。是故畏威，敬天也；式典，法祖也；靖四方，勤民也。君道孰有大於此三事者乎？周人一舉而兼盡之，周之德可謂至德也已矣。噫！此周家所以有道之長，而凡有天下國家者，尚其鑒之！

春秋

春，王正月，公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯侵蔡。蔡潰，遂伐楚，次于陘。楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵。〔僖公四年〕

馬出圖

考試官學正蔡，批〔序齊桓伐楚之績處深合傳意〕是邃於經學者。

考試官學正周，批〔謹嚴〕
translation_en:
…indeed. Sacrifice depends not on material offerings but on intent; thus one's appeal readily wins a response. It is not that I seek anything from the cultured ancestor. Spirits do not invariably accept offerings, but accept those made with sincerity and trustworthiness: their coming has a foundation. Do we not therefore have grounds to know that his acceptance of my offerings is certain? Ah! This may be called fully realizing the duty of attending to the unseen realm.

I have considered the Zhou people's sacrifice in the Hall of Enlightenment. The poem “Jiang xiang” [?] not only illuminates the sacrificial rites: in it we also find sincerity in revering Heaven, righteousness in emulating the ancestors, and beneficence in caring diligently for the people. Thus, to stand in awe of divine majesty is to revere Heaven; to follow established statutes is to emulate the ancestors; and to pacify the four quarters is to care diligently for the people. In the ruler's way, what could be greater than these three duties? The Zhou people fulfilled all three in a single act. Their virtue may indeed be called the highest virtue. Ah! This explains why the house of Zhou so long possessed the Way. May all who rule the realm or a state take it as their mirror!

Spring and Autumn Annals

In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke joined the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao in invading Cai. Cai collapsed. They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army; they concluded the covenant at Shaoling. 〔Fourth year of Duke Xi.〕

Ma Chutu

Examiner Cai, School Instructor, comments: 〔The passage recounting Duke Huan of Qi's achievement in attacking Chu accords closely with the meaning of the commentary.〕 This is someone deeply versed in classical learning.

Examiner Zhou, School Instructor, comments: 〔Careful and rigorous.〕

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
春秋序霸主攘夷之績有兵强而用之以律者
有敵服而待之以禮者此齊桓仗義服楚仁與
禮兼得之矣春秋隨事而序其績也固宜在昔
齊桓主霸銳意安攘當貫穀會盟之餘舉寔征
不庭之義爰合八國之諸侯先用奇兵侵蔡而
蔡衆以潰繼用正兵伐楚而楚人震恐是兵力
可謂强矣斯時也即使肆焉以逞而深入其阻
夫其雚固在我也桓則以爲與其殘吾民以事
攻伐孰若數文告而使之慴悟是故次止陘亭
===
蓋將先聲以伐其謀也兹其蓄威持重養銳休
兵固自有奪氣於未戰之先者矣噫自太原伐
而王師遠桓其振遺烈者乎春秋於伐楚之下
書次於陘傳所謂序其績者此也已而楚人恐
懼屈完惠來貢諾於包茅之入好承夫寡君之
願是敵人可謂服矣斯時也即使傲焉自處而
標諸轅門夫其勢亦在我也桓則以爲與其屈
以威而逼之面從孰若接以禮而使之心服是
故講盟召陵蓋治之以不治之法也兹其武功
punctuated: 春秋序霸主攘夷之績，有兵强而用之以律者，有敵服而待之以禮者。此齊桓仗義服楚，仁與禮兼得之矣，春秋隨事而序其績也固宜。在昔齊桓主霸，銳意安攘，當貫穀會盟之餘，舉寔征不庭之義，爰合八國之諸侯，先用奇兵侵蔡，而蔡衆以潰；繼用正兵伐楚，而楚人震恐，是兵力可謂强矣。斯時也，即使肆焉以逞而深入其阻，夫其雚固在我也。桓則以爲，與其殘吾民以事攻伐，孰若數文告而使之慴悟？是故次止陘亭，蓋將先聲以伐其謀也。兹其蓄威持重，養銳休兵，固自有奪氣於未戰之先者矣。噫！自太原伐而王師遠，桓其振遺烈者乎？春秋於伐楚之下書次於陘，傳所謂序其績者，此也。已而楚人恐懼，屈完惠來，貢諾於包茅之入，好承夫寡君之願，是敵人可謂服矣。斯時也，即使傲焉自處而標諸轅門，夫其勢亦在我也。桓則以爲，與其屈以威而逼之面從，孰若接以禮而使之心服？是故講盟召陵，蓋治之以不治之法也。兹其武功
translation_en: When the Spring and Autumn Annals recounts the achievements of hegemonic lords in repelling the barbarians, there are those who possess strong armies but employ them with discipline, and those whose enemies submit but who receive them with ritual propriety. In Duke Huan of Qi’s upholding righteousness and bringing Chu to submission, both benevolence and ritual propriety were attained. It is fitting, therefore, that the Spring and Autumn Annals should recount his achievements as each event occurred. Formerly, when Duke Huan of Qi held the hegemony, he was intent on securing peace within and repelling threats from without. Following the covenant assemblies at Guan and Gu, he invoked the principle of campaigning against those who failed to attend court. He accordingly brought together the lords of eight states. First he employed surprise troops to invade Cai, whose forces collapsed; then he employed regular troops to attack Chu, whose people trembled with fear. His military strength could indeed be called formidable. At that moment, even if he had given free rein to his ambition and penetrated deep into their difficult terrain, the advantage [?] would certainly have been his. Yet Duke Huan reasoned: rather than sacrifice my people in campaigns of attack, would it not be better to issue repeated proclamations and bring the enemy to a fearful awakening? He therefore halted and encamped at Xingting, intending to use the advance announcement of his demands to defeat their plans. By thus conserving his might and proceeding cautiously, nurturing his troops’ fighting spirit and giving them rest, he could assuredly break the enemy’s morale before battle. Ah! Since the expedition as far as Taiyuan, the days of the royal armies lay far in the past. Was Duke Huan not reviving their enduring achievements? After recording the attack on Chu, the Spring and Autumn Annals writes that he encamped at Xing. This is what the Commentary means by recounting his achievements. Subsequently, the people of Chu became afraid, and Qu Wan graciously came, pledging the delivery of bundled mao grass as tribute and cordially accepting the wishes of ‘our humble lord.’ The enemy could indeed be said to have submitted. At that moment, even if Duke Huan had assumed an arrogant posture and put Qu Wan on display at the camp gate, the power to do so would likewise have been his. Yet Duke Huan reasoned: rather than subdue him through force and compel outward obedience, would it not be better to receive him with ritual propriety and win his heartfelt submission? He therefore negotiated a covenant at Shaoling, governing them, in effect, through a method of refraining from punitive intervention. Thus, his martial achievement …

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
之戢文德之脩固將有攻心於不戰之外者矣
噫自因壘降而王事熄桓其程先民者乎春秋
書楚屈完來盟于師盟于召陵傳所謂序其績
者此也是則於師強敵服之時得退師待敵之
道故曰齊桓節制之兵也雖然桓公攘楚事則
善矣然攘夷狄所以尊周室也使其請命于周
奉行天討則名正言順而事成善之善也迺擅
合諸侯威行江漢豈所謂爲天吏則可以伐人
國哉是功雖多道不足尚也說者謂寧無齊桓
之功不可蹈齊桓不臣之咎噫韙而本之以正
此固用兵之法乎
夏楚人侵鄭〔宣公三年〕冬楚子伐鄭〔宣公四年〕
===
王里
考試官學正蔡　批〔題本平易作者非腐則泛此篇閎嚴義正良史之才也錄之〕
考試官學正周　批〔筆力老健〕
小爽非義以虐貳國春秋罪之仗義以討貳國
punctuated:
之戢、文德之脩，固將有攻心於不戰之外者矣。噫！自因壘降而王事熄，桓其程先民者乎？《春秋》書「楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵」，傳所謂「序其績」者，此也。是則於師強敵服之時，得退師待敵之道，故曰：「齊桓節制之兵也。」雖然，桓公攘楚，事則善矣。然攘夷狄，所以尊周室也。使其請命于周，奉行天討，則名正言順而事成，善之善也。迺擅合諸侯，威行江漢，豈所謂「爲天吏則可以伐人國」哉？是功雖多，道不足尚也。說者謂：「寧無齊桓之功，不可蹈齊桓不臣之咎。」噫！韙而本之以正，此固用兵之法乎！
夏，楚人侵鄭。〔宣公三年〕冬，楚子伐鄭。〔宣公四年〕
王里
考試官學正蔡，批〔題本平易，作者非腐則泛。此篇閎嚴義正，良史之才也，錄之。〕
考試官學正周，批〔筆力老健。〕
小爽非義以虐貳國，《春秋》罪之；仗義以討貳國，
translation_en:
…the restraint of military might and the cultivation of civil virtue would surely win hearts without resorting to battle. Ah! Since the surrender at the ramparts [?] brought the royal undertaking to an end, was Duke Huan perhaps taking the ancients as his model? The Spring and Autumn Annals records: “Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army; they made the covenant at Shaoling.” This is what the commentary means by “setting forth his achievements.” Thus, when his army was strong and the enemy had submitted, he understood how to withdraw his forces and treat the enemy. Hence the saying: “Duke Huan of Qi’s army was governed by restraint and discipline.”
Nevertheless, although Duke Huan’s repulsion of Chu was a good deed, the purpose of repelling the Yi and Di was to honor the royal house of Zhou. Had he requested a command from Zhou and carried out Heaven’s punitive expedition, his standing would have been legitimate, his words proper, and his undertaking successful—the best of good deeds. Instead, he assembled the regional lords on his own authority and exerted his might in the regions of the Yangzi and Han rivers. Could this be what is meant by “Only one who acts as Heaven’s officer may attack another’s state”? Thus, however numerous his achievements, his way does not merit esteem. A commentator says: “Better to lack Duke Huan of Qi’s achievements than to incur his guilt of failing in a subject’s duty.” Ah! To do what is right and ground it in rectitude—is this not indeed the proper method of employing troops?
“In summer, men of Chu invaded Zheng.” 〔Third year of Duke Xuan.〕 “In winter, the Viscount of Chu attacked Zheng.” 〔Fourth year of Duke Xuan.〕
Wang Li
Examiner Cai, School Instructor, comments: 〔The topic is straightforward, but writers tend to be either stale or diffuse. This piece is expansive yet rigorous, and sound in its interpretation: it shows the talent of a fine historian. Include it in the record.〕
Examiner Zhou, School Instructor, comments: 〔The writing is seasoned and vigorous.〕
To deviate slightly [?] and act unjustly to oppress a state of divided allegiance is condemned by the Spring and Autumn Annals; to uphold righteousness in punishing a state of divided allegiance …

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
春秋予之此楚莊兩加兵於鄭春秋抑揚其詞
所以嚴大防而謹大倫也爲何如嘗考鄭居晉
楚之衝而從違之間夷夏之盛衰關焉迺宣公
三年之夏楚人侵鄭或謂其與後此伐鄭一也
其稱人與侵者何蓋夷夏大防也自鄭穆背楚
服從於晉人方幸其不遠之復矣是果可以兵
脅之也與哉于何莊也知鄭之足以重楚而不
知楚之不可以有鄭知勢之足以得鄭而不知
理之不可以從楚必欲恃强暴而逼之爲已屬
===
焉其於先王五服之制不亦有乖乎哉夫易晝
否泰所以嚴內外之防也楚敢舉其防而決之
不謂之敢行稱亂可乎春秋書楚人侵鄭則莊
之罪不可掩而鄭穆惠迪之吉亦因以著矣迨
夫四年之冬楚復伐鄭或謂其與前此侵鄭一
也其稱爵以伐者何蓋君父大倫也自歸生弑
逆諸侯莫討人方慮其彝倫之攸斁矣是果可
以幸免之也與哉孰意楚也以踈遠之夷而憂
及中國諸侯之事率荆蠻之衆而正其弑父與
punctuated:
春秋予之。此楚莊兩加兵於鄭，春秋抑揚其詞，所以嚴大防而謹大倫也，爲何如？嘗考鄭居晉楚之衝，而從違之間，夷夏之盛衰關焉。迺宣公三年之夏，楚人侵鄭。或謂其與後此伐鄭一也，其稱人與侵者何？蓋夷夏大防也。自鄭穆背楚，服從於晉，人方幸其不遠之復矣。是果可以兵脅之也與哉？于何莊也，知鄭之足以重楚，而不知楚之不可以有鄭；知勢之足以得鄭，而不知理之不可以從楚，必欲恃强暴而逼之爲已屬焉。其於先王五服之制，不亦有乖乎哉？夫易晝否泰，所以嚴內外之防也。楚敢舉其防而決之，不謂之敢行稱亂可乎？春秋書楚人侵鄭，則莊之罪不可掩，而鄭穆惠迪之吉亦因以著矣。
迨夫四年之冬，楚復伐鄭。或謂其與前此侵鄭一也，其稱爵以伐者何？蓋君父大倫也。自歸生弑逆，諸侯莫討，人方慮其彝倫之攸斁矣。是果可以幸免之也與哉？孰意楚也，以踈遠之夷，而憂及中國諸侯之事；率荆蠻之衆，而正其弑父與
translation_en:
…the Spring and Autumn Annals approves it. In these two instances when King Zhuang of Chu took up arms against Zheng, how did the Annals, through its disparaging and approving language, uphold the great boundary and safeguard the cardinal relationships? I have examined how Zheng lay at the strategic junction between Jin and Chu: its choice of allegiance or resistance bore upon the rise and decline of the non-Hua peoples and the Xia states. In the summer of Duke Xuan’s third year, “men of Chu invaded Zheng.” Some say this was the same as the subsequent campaign against Zheng. Why, then, does the text use “men” and “invaded”? Because of the great boundary between the non-Hua peoples and the Xia states. After Duke Mu of Zheng turned away from Chu and submitted to Jin, people were rejoicing that he had returned before straying far. Could it truly be right to threaten him with armed force? Why was it that King Zhuang knew Zheng could enhance Chu’s importance, yet did not know that Chu had no right to possess Zheng; knew that force could secure Zheng, yet did not know that principle forbade Zheng to follow Chu? He insisted on relying on violence to compel Zheng to become his subordinate. Did this not contravene the former kings’ system of five zones of service? The Book of Changes delineates [?] the hexagrams Obstruction and Peace to maintain strictly the boundary between inner and outer. Chu dared to break down that boundary: could one fail to call this brazenly fomenting disorder [?]? When the Annals records “men of Chu invaded Zheng,” King Zhuang’s guilt cannot be concealed, while the good fortune attending Duke Mu of Zheng’s adherence to the proper way is thereby also made manifest.
In the winter of the fourth year, Chu again campaigned against Zheng. Some say this was the same as the earlier invasion of Zheng. Why, then, does the text designate Chu’s ruler by his noble rank and use “campaigned against”? Because of the cardinal relationships involving ruler and father. After Guisheng committed regicide and rebellion, none of the feudal lords punished him, and people were anxious that the enduring moral relationships were being destroyed. Could he truly be allowed to escape punishment through good fortune? Who would have expected Chu, a distant non-Hua state, to concern itself with the affairs of the feudal lords of the Central States, and to lead the hosts of Jing’s non-Hua peoples to punish the crime of murdering one’s father and …

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
君之惡雖未執其人而麗之於刑焉其於司馬
九伐之法不亦有光乎哉夫禮重殘執所以嚴
亂賊之戒也楚能舉其義而振之不謂之禮失
求之野可乎春秋書楚子伐鄭則莊之善不容
泯而諸侯之罪亦因以明矣觀諸此則春秋謹
華夷之辨嚴亂賊之黨一字爲襃貶不亦深切
著明也哉雖然楚非能討賊者也特假之以行
其私耳聖人與之者扶天常立人紀不得已之
意也其後入陳圍鄭敗晉滅蕭矜其威力以恐
===
中國無非以力假仁之事豈誠於爲善者哉君
子於此又當知春秋不得已而予楚之意
禮記
君子耆老不徒行庶人耆老不徒食
王惟一
同考試官學正龍 批 此題乃王道之成作者類本
吉于能體認用賢昬親親入講深得化民成俗之意是宜錄之
考試官學正蔡 批 善形容盛世氣象
考試官學正周 批 莊重古雅
punctuated:
君之惡，雖未執其人而麗之於刑焉，其於司馬九伐之法，不亦有光乎哉？夫禮重殘執，所以嚴亂賊之戒也。楚能舉其義而振之，不謂之禮失求之野可乎？春秋書楚子伐鄭，則莊之善不容泯，而諸侯之罪亦因以明矣。觀諸此，則春秋謹華夷之辨，嚴亂賊之黨，一字爲襃貶，不亦深切著明也哉？雖然，楚非能討賊者也，特假之以行其私耳。聖人與之者，扶天常、立人紀，不得已之意也。其後入陳、圍鄭、敗晉、滅蕭，矜其威力以恐中國，無非以力假仁之事，豈誠於爲善者哉？君子於此，又當知春秋不得已而予楚之意。

禮記
君子耆老不徒行，庶人耆老不徒食。
王惟一

同考試官學正龍批：此題乃王道之成，作者類本吉于能體認用賢昬親親入講，深得化民成俗之意，是宜錄之。
考試官學正蔡批：善形容盛世氣象。
考試官學正周批：莊重古雅。
translation_en:
…and ruler. Although he had not seized the culprit and subjected him to punishment, did this not bring lustre to the Minister of War’s rules for the nine kinds of punitive expedition? Ritual places weight on destroying and capturing wrongdoers [?], thereby sternly warning rebels and traitors. Since Chu could uphold and give force to this principle, could this not be called seeking among the uncultivated what has been lost in ritual practice? The Spring and Autumn Annals records, “The Viscount of Chu attacked Zheng.” Thus King Zhuang’s good deed cannot be effaced, while the guilt of the feudal lords is thereby also made plain. Viewed in this light, the Spring and Autumn Annals carefully maintains the distinction between the Chinese and the barbarians and sternly judges the accomplices of rebels and traitors. Does its use of a single word to confer praise or blame not convey a profound, incisive, and unmistakable judgment?

Nevertheless, Chu was not truly capable of punishing traitors; it merely used this as a pretext to pursue its own interests. The sage’s approval of it expressed his reluctant intention to uphold Heaven’s enduring norms and establish the fundamental bonds of human society. Later, Chu entered Chen, besieged Zheng, defeated Jin, and destroyed Xiao, vaunting its military might to intimidate the central states. These were all instances of using force under the guise of benevolence. How could Chu have been sincere in doing good? Here the gentleman should also understand why the Spring and Autumn Annals accorded Chu approval only out of necessity.

Record of Rites
“When gentlemen grow old, they do not travel on foot; when commoners grow old, they do not eat their meals without accompanying dishes.”
Wang Weiyi

Associate Examiner Long, School Instructor, comments: “This topic concerns the fulfillment of the Kingly Way. The author appears to take as his basis [?] an understanding of employing the worthy and showing affection to one’s kin in developing his exposition [?]. He profoundly grasps the intention of transforming the people and establishing good customs. This answer therefore merits inclusion.”

Examiner Cai, School Instructor, comments: “Skillfully depicts the atmosphere of a flourishing age.”

Examiner Zhou, School Instructor, comments: “Grave and dignified, with classical elegance.”

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
老者各得其所安而王道成矣夫老者安之王
道之所以成也豈可以易而致哉治天下者宜
知所務矣記王制者謂夫爲治之道莫備於王
政王政之施莫先於養老然天下之老若是其
衆也豈家爲之給而人爲之圖哉必有所以致
之者矣故當其時有君子之耆老焉齒可尚德
亦可尊若人也蓋嘗定之位授之任而以不徒
行爲安者也使倫制未盡則賢賢之義隱矣欲
其必乘而行得乎王者之世所用惟賢而所好
===
惟德則命車乘馬以別於凡民無行而不遂其
心者明有賢也人賢其賢而君子之老得所安
者盡天下矣有庶人之耆老焉不惟其德惟其
齒若人也蓋雖無常職無常祿而以不徒食爲
安者也使教養未備則親親之恩塞矣欲其必
羞而食可乎王者之民既厚於生而又敏于行
則貳膳常珍以篤於愛敬無食而不順其志者
知有親也各親其親而庶人之老得所安者盡
天下矣夫君子以行言則可以兼庶人之養庶
punctuated: 老者各得其所安，而王道成矣。夫老者安之，王道之所以成也，豈可以易而致哉？治天下者宜知所務矣。記王制者謂夫爲治之道，莫備於王政；王政之施，莫先於養老。然天下之老，若是其衆也，豈家爲之給而人爲之圖哉？必有所以致之者矣。故當其時，有君子之耆老焉，齒可尚，德亦可尊。若人也，蓋嘗定之位，授之任，而以不徒行爲安者也。使倫制未盡，則賢賢之義隱矣，欲其必乘而行，得乎？王者之世，所用惟賢，而所好惟德，則命車乘馬，以別於凡民，無行而不遂其心者，明有賢也。人賢其賢，而君子之老得所安者盡天下矣。有庶人之耆老焉，不惟其德，惟其齒。若人也，蓋雖無常職、無常祿，而以不徒食爲安者也。使教養未備，則親親之恩塞矣，欲其必羞而食，可乎？王者之民，既厚於生，而又敏于行，則貳膳常珍，以篤於愛敬，無食而不順其志者，知有親也。各親其親，而庶人之老得所安者盡天下矣。夫君子以行言，則可以兼庶人之養；庶
translation_en:
When the elderly each obtain the comfort appropriate to them, the Kingly Way is fulfilled. Providing comfort for the elderly is what brings the Kingly Way to fulfillment. Could this be achieved easily? Those who govern the realm should know where to direct their efforts. The author of the “Royal Regulations” says that no way of governing is more comprehensive than kingly government, and in implementing kingly government nothing takes precedence over caring for the elderly. Yet the elderly throughout the realm are so numerous: could one supply them household by household and make provision for them person by person? There must be a means of bringing this about.

Thus, in that age there were elderly gentlemen whose years merited esteem and whose virtue also deserved honor. Such men had been assigned positions and entrusted with responsibilities, and their comfort lay in not having to travel on foot. If the institutions governing social relationships were not fully realized, the duty of honoring the worthy would be obscured. Could one then expect them always to have a conveyance when they traveled? In the age of a true king, only the worthy are employed and only virtue is cherished. Accordingly, carriages bestowed by royal command and teams of horses distinguish them from ordinary people. That their wishes are fulfilled whenever they travel makes manifest the recognition of worthiness. When people honor those worthy of honor, elderly gentlemen throughout the realm obtain the comfort appropriate to them.

There were also elderly commoners. Regard was paid not to their virtue but to their years. Although such people had neither permanent office nor regular emoluments, their comfort lay in not eating a meal without accompanying dishes. If instruction and material provision were incomplete, the affection expressed in cherishing one’s kin would be obstructed. Could one then expect them always to have savory dishes with their meals? The people of a true king are amply provided for in their livelihood and also diligent in their conduct. They therefore provide additional dishes and regular delicacies to deepen their love and respect. That every meal accords with the elders’ wishes shows an understanding of the claims of kinship. When everyone cherishes their own kin, elderly commoners throughout the realm obtain the comfort appropriate to them.

Now, when gentlemen are spoken of in terms of travel, this can also encompass the sustenance provided to commoners; as for commoners…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
人以食言則不必並君子之尊理本一也是故
凡爲老者皆有安之理焉分則殊也是故凡所
安者必隨其老之分爲理周於分之外分析於
理之中王道之大有如是夫噫推此義也將無
一物不得其所矣嘗觀之詩何君子而强仕者
賦兎爰之咏庶人而力耕者懷葛藟之憂視王
者之民相懸若是孟子稱文王善養老不過制
之恒產敎之樹畜道之使自爲養而天下之老
以爲已歸其告齊梁實本於此然視民如傷文
===
王何心也豈惠宣所得與哉文王非知民之無
傷姑爲是退抑謙冲而已誠慮夫一民之不得
其所而弗恐安是故惠鮮懷保以至于咸和豈
自以爲足哉夫固所謂聖人之心也是故有聖
人之心而後有聖人之仁
禮樂刑政四達而不悖則王道備矣
仇炅
同考試官學正龍　批　〔聖王之節人情禮樂爲本此作〕
〔爲輔此作且能闡禮樂之精微非徒習聲容器數之末者宜式多士〕
punctuated:
人以食言，則不必並君子之尊。理本一也，是故凡爲老者，皆有安之理焉；分則殊也，是故凡所安者，必隨其老之分爲。理周於分之外，分析於理之中，王道之大有如是夫！噫！推此義也，將無一物不得其所矣。嘗觀之《詩》，何君子而强仕者賦《兎爰》之咏，庶人而力耕者懷《葛藟》之憂？視王者之民，相懸若是！孟子稱文王善養老，不過制之恒產，敎之樹畜，道之使自爲養，而天下之老以爲已歸。其告齊梁，實本於此。然視民如傷，文王何心也？豈惠宣所得與哉！文王非知民之無傷，姑爲是退抑謙冲而已，誠慮夫一民之不得其所而弗恐安。是故惠鮮懷保，以至于咸和，豈自以爲足哉？夫固所謂聖人之心也。是故有聖人之心，而後有聖人之仁。
禮樂刑政四達而不悖，則王道備矣。
仇炅
同考試官學正龍，批：〔聖王之節人情禮樂爲本此作〕〔爲輔此作且能闡禮樂之精微非徒習聲容器數之末者宜式多士〕
translation_en:
…when commoners are spoken of in terms of their sustenance, they need not also receive the honors accorded to gentlemen. The principle is fundamentally one; thus all who are old have a rightful claim to peaceful care. Their stations, however, differ; thus the care provided must accord with each elderly person's station. Principle extends beyond distinctions of station, while distinctions of station are differentiated within principle. Such is the greatness of the Kingly Way! Ah! Extend this meaning, and nothing will fail to find its proper place. I have considered the Book of Odes: why do gentlemen in the prime of service voice the lament of “The Hare” (Tu yuan), while commoners laboring at the plow harbor the sorrow of “The Creeping Vines” (Ge lei)? How far removed their condition is from that of the people under a true king! When Mengzi praised King Wen for caring well for the aged, this meant no more than securing them a constant livelihood, teaching them to plant trees and raise livestock, and guiding them to provide for themselves. Yet the aged throughout the realm felt that they had found a home with him. Mengzi's counsel to Qi and Liang was indeed founded upon this. But what heart did King Wen possess, that he regarded the people as though they were wounded? How could Kings Hui and Xuan match it? King Wen did not know the people to be unharmed and merely adopt this restrained and humble attitude. He truly feared that even one person might fail to find a proper place, and could not rest at ease [?]. Thus he bestowed kindness on the needy and cherished and protected the people, until all were in harmony. How could he consider his efforts sufficient? This is precisely what is called the heart of a sage. Thus only after possessing a sage's heart can one possess a sage's benevolence.
When ritual, music, punishments, and government all operate unhindered and without conflict, the Kingly Way is complete.
Qiu Jiong
Comment by Associate Examiner Long, School Instructor: 〔In the sage king's regulation of human feelings, ritual and music are the foundation. This composition…〕〔…serve as auxiliaries [?]. This composition can also elucidate the subtle essence of ritual and music; it does more than rehearse the superficial details of sounds, ceremonial deportment, implements, and numerical prescriptions. It should serve as a model for the assembled scholars.〕

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
考試官學正蔡　批〔精確〕
考試官學正周　批〔備于發揮尤詣〕
純乎王道者治之至也夫禮樂刑政王者爲治
之道也達之天下則天下治矣非純乎道者其
孰能與於此記樂者曰天下之不一者人而至
一者心不同者事而大同者理感以心未嘗不
通觸以理未嘗不應王者慮夫人之物誘深而
好惡無節也制爲禮樂輔以刑政其義則因事
而異名其究則殊途而同歸見其禮志可道也
===
聞其樂聲可和也感而動者之用管乎人情矣
以一其行以防其姦敢或違乎可以合敬器數
不與焉可以同愛聲容不與焉生而静者之體
準諸四海矣罔干于政不犯于刑何悖之有夫
禮樂以致中和之化驗諸刑政而不窮刑政以
盡鼓舞之神徵之禮樂而益順是豈法制形跡
爲藻飾太平之具耶抑豈聲音笑貌爲取辦小
補之功耶道本如是其純而王之所以爲王者
也存之則純王之心發之則純王之政雖曰大
punctuated:
考試官學正蔡，批〔精確〕。
考試官學正周，批〔備于發揮尤詣〕。
純乎王道者，治之至也。夫禮樂刑政，王者爲治之道也。達之天下，則天下治矣。非純乎道者，其孰能與於此？記樂者曰：天下之不一者人，而至一者心；不同者事，而大同者理。感以心，未嘗不通；觸以理，未嘗不應。王者慮夫人之物誘深而好惡無節也，制爲禮樂，輔以刑政。其義則因事而異名，其究則殊途而同歸。見其禮，志可道也；聞其樂，聲可和也。感而動者之用，管乎人情矣。以一其行，以防其姦，敢或違乎？可以合敬，器數不與焉；可以同愛，聲容不與焉。生而静者之體，準諸四海矣。罔干于政，不犯于刑，何悖之有？夫禮樂以致中和之化，驗諸刑政而不窮；刑政以盡鼓舞之神，徵之禮樂而益順。是豈法制形跡爲藻飾太平之具耶？抑豈聲音笑貌爲取辦小補之功耶？道本如是其純，而王之所以爲王者也。存之則純王之心，發之則純王之政。雖曰大
translation_en:
Examiner Cai, Instructor, comments: 〔Precise and sound.〕
Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: 〔Comprehensive in its exposition and especially accomplished [?].〕
Purity in the kingly Way is the highest achievement of government. Ritual, music, punishments, and administration are the means by which a true king governs. When they extend throughout the realm, the realm is well governed. Who could attain this without being pure in the Way? The recorder of music says: What differs throughout the world is people, but what is wholly one is the heart; what varies is affairs, but what is universally shared is principle. When moved through the heart, people never fail to communicate; when touched through principle, they never fail to respond. The king, concerned that people are deeply enticed by external things and that their likes and dislikes lack restraint, establishes ritual and music and supplements them with punishments and administration. In their significance, these bear different names according to the affairs they address; in their ultimate effect, they reach the same destination by different paths. Seeing his rituals, people’s intentions can be guided; hearing his music, their voices can be harmonized. Thus the functioning of what moves in response to stimulation brings human feelings under control. With conduct unified and wrongdoing prevented, would anyone dare transgress? People can be united in reverence without dependence on ritual vessels and prescribed numbers; they can share in love without dependence on sounds and ceremonial movements. Thus the substance of what is still at birth becomes the standard throughout the Four Seas. None contravenes the administration or incurs punishment: what discord could there be? Ritual and music bring about the transforming influence of equilibrium and harmony, and their efficacy, tested in punishments and administration, is inexhaustible. Punishments and administration fully realize the wondrous power to inspire people, and, measured against ritual and music, become still more harmonious. Could these merely be laws, institutions, and outward forms used to embellish an age of peace? Or could they merely be pleasing voices and smiling faces employed to secure some small benefit? The Way is inherently pure in this manner, and this is what makes a king a true king. Preserved within, it is the heart of pure kingship; expressed outwardly, it is the government of pure kingship. Though one speaks of a great…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
業當有若不足以盡之然情不可變以統同也
理不可易以辨異也禮樂舉而天地昭大人之
能事畢矣用休用威亦範圍之中耳治道由是
而出何加焉盛德日新似不止於此者然殊時
不相沿本無聲也異世不相襲本無體也禮樂
備而天地官聖神之功化極矣以懲以勸亦曲
成之下耳民心由是而同孰禦焉是則先王之
治質之理而當即之心而安有弗感感斯通有
弗觸觸斯應信乎治道莫備於此而何以他求
===
爲哉雖然樂著不息爲天禮著不動爲地而大
禮與天地同節大樂與天地同和則天地禮樂
亦一而已聖人兼明聖之德探述作之原通陰
陽之義貫動靜之理則裁成輔相以收位育之
功取諸心焉耳孰謂古禮之不可復而今樂之
不可變哉彼刑政而已者霸之所以霸也周禮
在魯韶樂在齊無補春秋之治抑末矣故曰履
中正而樂和平
第貳場
punctuated:
業，當有若不足以盡之。然情不可變，以統同也；理不可易，以辨異也。禮樂舉而天地昭，大人之能事畢矣；用休用威，亦範圍之中耳。治道由是而出，何加焉？盛德日新，似不止於此者。然殊時不相沿，本無聲也；異世不相襲，本無體也。禮樂備而天地官，聖神之功化極矣；以懲以勸，亦曲成之下耳。民心由是而同，孰禦焉？是則先王之治，質之理而當，即之心而安。有弗感，感斯通；有弗觸，觸斯應。信乎治道莫備於此，而何以他求爲哉？雖然，樂著不息爲天，禮著不動爲地，而大禮與天地同節，大樂與天地同和，則天地禮樂亦一而已。聖人兼明聖之德，探述作之原，通陰陽之義，貫動靜之理，則裁成輔相以收位育之功，取諸心焉耳。孰謂古禮之不可復，而今樂之不可變哉？彼刑政而已者，霸之所以霸也。周禮在魯，韶樂在齊，無補春秋之治，抑末矣。故曰：「履中正而樂和平。」

第貳場
translation_en:
…undertaking might seem insufficient to encompass it fully. Yet the feelings cannot be changed, for they unite what is alike; the principles cannot be altered, for they distinguish what differs. When ritual and music are put into practice and Heaven and Earth shine forth, the great man's full capacity has been realized. The use of favor and of awe also falls within their encompassing scope. The Way of government proceeds from this: what could be added? Abundant virtue is renewed daily and seems to extend beyond this. Yet different ages do not simply continue one another's practices, for music originally has no fixed sound; successive eras do not merely copy one another, for ritual originally has no fixed form. When ritual and music are complete and Heaven and Earth perform their offices, the transformative achievements of sagely and spiritual wisdom reach their utmost extent. Punishment and encouragement, too, fall within their work of bringing each thing to fulfillment. Through this the people's hearts are united: who could resist it? Thus the government of the former kings proves fitting when tested against principle and brings peace when referred to the heart. There may be no stirring, but once stirred, there is communion; there may be no contact, but once touched, there is response. Truly, the Way of government is nowhere more complete than here. Why seek it elsewhere?

Nevertheless, music manifests ceaseless activity and thus corresponds to Heaven; ritual manifests stillness and thus corresponds to Earth. Great ritual shares the ordering measures of Heaven and Earth, and great music shares their harmony. Heaven, Earth, ritual, and music are therefore one. The sage combines the virtues of illumination and sageliness, investigates the origins of transmitting and creating, comprehends the meaning of yin and yang, and penetrates the principles of movement and stillness. In shaping and assisting the workings of Heaven and Earth to achieve the proper positioning and nourishment of all things, he draws only upon the heart. Who says that ancient ritual cannot be restored or present-day music changed? Reliance on punishments and administration alone is what makes a hegemon merely a hegemon. The ritual of Zhou survived in Lu, and the Shao music survived in Qi, yet they did nothing to aid government in the Spring and Autumn period: these were merely the outward remnants. Hence the saying: “Tread the path of centrality and correctness, and delight in peace and harmony.”

Second Session

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
論
至仁則天地為一身　路王道
同考試官教諭彭　批　〔格局步驟雋永圓融且引經証傳無支離詆道莊老緣之學健羨健羨〕
同考試官教諭崔　批　〔通篇明白正大學有源委才能斷制于立論間見之〕
考試官學正蔡　批　得立言本意
考試官學正周　批　莊重渾融
===
聖人之心以己視天下故亦以天下視己以己
視天下則必以所以處身者而處天下以天下
視己則凡有所歉于天下亦吾身之累也嗚呼
聖人之心何其至仁之若是哉蓋其分量固大
而察乎天地者固審也何者天地有所不忍于
物而亦無所擇于物也聖人合德于天地者也
故其心有所不忍于身亦必有所不忍于天下
而無所擇于天下者亦猶夫無所擇于其身也
聖人者仁之至也仁則公公則無我矣無我則
punctuated:
論

至仁則天地為一身。路王道。

同考試官教諭彭批：〔格局步驟，雋永圓融，且引經証傳，無支離詆道莊老緣之學，健羨健羨！〕

同考試官教諭崔批：〔通篇明白正大，學有源委，才能斷制，于立論間見之。〕

考試官學正蔡批：得立言本意。

考試官學正周批：莊重渾融。

聖人之心，以己視天下，故亦以天下視己。以己視天下，則必以所以處身者而處天下；以天下視己，則凡有所歉于天下，亦吾身之累也。嗚呼！聖人之心，何其至仁之若是哉！蓋其分量固大，而察乎天地者固審也。何者？天地有所不忍于物，而亦無所擇于物也。聖人合德于天地者也，故其心有所不忍于身，亦必有所不忍于天下；而無所擇于天下者，亦猶夫無所擇于其身也。聖人者，仁之至也。仁則公，公則無我矣，無我則
translation_en:
Discourse

“With Perfect Benevolence, Heaven and Earth Form a Single Body.” By Lu Wangdao.

Comment by Associate Examiner Peng, Instructor: 〔“The structure and progression are rich in lasting significance and smoothly integrated. Moreover, it cites the classics to substantiate the commentaries, without disjointedness; the passage concerning disparagement of the Way and the learning of Zhuangzi and Laozi is unclear [?]. Admirable, admirable!”〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Cui, Instructor: 〔“The entire piece is lucid, upright, and dignified. The author's learning has both source and development; his ability and decisiveness emerge in the course of his argument.”〕

Comment by Examiner Cai, School Instructor: “It grasps the original intent of the statement.”

Comment by Examiner Zhou, School Instructor: “Dignified and thoroughly integrated.”

The sage's heart views all under Heaven as his own self, and therefore also views his own self in terms of all under Heaven. Viewing all under Heaven as his own self, he necessarily treats it as he treats his own person. Viewing his own self in terms of all under Heaven, he regards any failure in his obligations toward the world as a burden upon his own person. Ah! How consummate is the benevolence of the sage's heart! Surely its capacity is vast, and its discernment of Heaven and Earth is exact. Why is this? Heaven and Earth cannot bear to see creatures suffer, yet make no distinctions among them. The sage unites his virtue with Heaven and Earth. Thus, just as his heart cannot bear suffering in his own person, it necessarily cannot bear suffering anywhere under Heaven. His refusal to make distinctions among those under Heaven is likewise comparable to his refusal to make distinctions among the parts of his own person. The sage embodies benevolence at its utmost. Benevolence brings impartiality; impartiality brings freedom from self. With no self, then…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
無物矣而天也地也我也一也聯屬以成身而
一心之範圍運之而無外矣蓋至是而浩乎莫
見其大眇乎莫見其小宇宙內事卽吾方寸內
事也茲固至仁之量也歟善乎程子之言曰至
仁則天地爲一身可謂知聖人之心者矣世之
言仁以愛者皆曰愛莫大于吾身言愛則是而
言身則非也蓋愛之爲義大而身之爲言有非
尺寸之膚之謂也故愛以己專虧仁之體者也
尺寸以爲膚自視小者也彼其自小也吾無足
===
異而獨情夫私之未融而見之未廣也于是乎
爲狥世物一膜之外卽爲胡越其視天地判乎
其不相關而仁之道或幾乎熄矣甚哉小見之
不可以言仁也昔者夫子之告子貢曰仁者己
欲立而立人己欲達而達人其言博施濟衆也
猶病于堯舜夫立必俱立得必俱得達必俱達
成不獨成仁之本體則然矣而博施濟衆堯舜
之能事也顧以爲病焉豈聖人自歉于力之不
能而不足以一身天地哉蓋聖人之心施必博
punctuated: 無物矣，而天也、地也、我也，一也，聯屬以成身，而一心之範圍運之而無外矣。蓋至是而浩乎莫見其大，眇乎莫見其小，宇宙內事卽吾方寸內事也。茲固至仁之量也歟？善乎程子之言曰：「至仁則天地爲一身。」可謂知聖人之心者矣。世之言仁以愛者，皆曰愛莫大于吾身。言愛則是，而言身則非也。蓋愛之爲義大，而身之爲言，有非尺寸之膚之謂也。故愛以己專，虧仁之體者也；尺寸以爲膚，自視小者也。彼其自小也，吾無足異，而獨情夫私之未融而見之未廣也。于是乎爲狥世物，一膜之外卽爲胡越，其視天地判乎其不相關，而仁之道或幾乎熄矣。甚哉，小見之不可以言仁也！昔者夫子之告子貢曰：「仁者己欲立而立人，己欲達而達人。」其言博施濟衆也，猶病于堯舜。夫立必俱立，得必俱得，達必俱達，成不獨成，仁之本體則然矣。而博施濟衆，堯舜之能事也，顧以爲病焉。豈聖人自歉于力之不能，而不足以一身天地哉？蓋聖人之心，施必博
translation_en: …there is no longer any distinction from things. Heaven, earth, and I are one, joined together to constitute a single body; the encompassing activity of the one mind leaves nothing outside it. At this point, its vastness is such that none can discern its full extent, and its minuteness such that none can discern its smallness. Affairs within the universe are precisely affairs within my own heart. Is this not indeed the capacity of consummate benevolence? Well did Master Cheng say: “With consummate benevolence, heaven and earth form one body.” He may truly be said to have understood the mind of the sage. Those in the world who explain benevolence in terms of love all say that no love is greater than love for one's own body. In speaking of love they are right; in speaking of the body they are wrong. For the meaning of love is vast, and what is meant by “body” is something other than these few inches of skin. Thus, to reserve love exclusively for oneself diminishes the substance of benevolence; to regard one's skin as merely a matter of inches [?] is to take a small view of oneself. That they belittle themselves gives me no cause for wonder; I only lament [?] that their selfishness has not dissolved and their vision has not broadened. Consequently, they become followers of worldly things: everything beyond a single membrane becomes as alien as the Hu and the Yue. They regard heaven and earth as utterly separate from themselves and unrelated to them, until the Way of benevolence is almost extinguished. How profoundly such narrow vision disqualifies one from speaking of benevolence! Formerly, the Master told Zigong: “The benevolent person, wishing to establish himself, establishes others; wishing to attain success himself, enables others to attain success.” Speaking of bestowing benefits widely and aiding the multitude, he said that even Yao and Shun found this difficult. For when one is established, all must be established; when one gains something, all must gain it; when one succeeds, all must succeed; accomplishment cannot belong to oneself alone. Such is the fundamental substance of benevolence. Bestowing benefits widely and aiding the multitude were achievements within the powers of Yao and Shun, yet even they found this difficult. Could it be that the sages felt dissatisfied with the inadequacy of their powers, as though these were insufficient to form one body with heaven and earth? For in the mind of the sage, the bestowal of benefits must be broad…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
濟必衆而後快也而庸有一夫之不獲則有以
病吾天地一體之義而若爲是不能釋然者知
堯舜以博施濟衆爲病則至仁之所以體天地
者不能已矣何則天地之生物也知以大始作
以成物其吹爲風呵爲霧怒爲慘喜爲舒鼓之
以雷霆潤之以雨露息之以晝夜而無所不用
其極是天地之于萬物若有所不容解于其心
者也茲固其至仁也而聖人則踐形惟肖者也
故無私如天地而至仁與之並故不以已之一
===
身爲身而以天地之浩乎莫窮者爲身不便乎
已之自安而于物之得所者恒致意也嗚呼聖
人之心何其愛之廣而量之大哉聖人于天下
誠有所不忍于心焉者也今夫人之于重器也
措諸善地而猶藉之茅何者愛器之心始之也
而況于其身乎培持之以壽其源粱肉之以育
其生藥石之以祛其疾因時致宜以豫其內外
之養者靡不至矣故指不若人則求伸不遠于
秦楚以吾身所屬也手足痿痺而心弗之覺則
punctuated:
濟必衆而後快也。而庸有一夫之不獲，則有以病吾天地一體之義，而若爲是不能釋然者。知堯舜以博施濟衆爲病，則至仁之所以體天地者不能已矣。何則？天地之生物也，知以大始，作以成物。其吹爲風，呵爲霧，怒爲慘，喜爲舒，鼓之以雷霆，潤之以雨露，息之以晝夜，而無所不用其極。是天地之于萬物，若有所不容解于其心者也。茲固其至仁也，而聖人則踐形惟肖者也。故無私如天地，而至仁與之並。故不以已之一身爲身，而以天地之浩乎莫窮者爲身；不便乎已之自安，而于物之得所者恒致意也。
嗚呼！聖人之心，何其愛之廣而量之大哉！聖人于天下，誠有所不忍于心焉者也。今夫人之于重器也，措諸善地而猶藉之茅。何者？愛器之心始之也。而況于其身乎？培持之以壽其源，粱肉之以育其生，藥石之以祛其疾，因時致宜以豫其內外之養者，靡不至矣。故指不若人則求伸，不遠于秦楚，以吾身所屬也。手足痿痺而心弗之覺，則
translation_en:
…and only when the multitudes have been aided is he satisfied. If even a single person should fail to obtain his due, this troubles my sense of forming one body with Heaven and Earth, leaving me unable to rest easy. Once we understand that Yao and Shun regarded giving broadly and aiding the multitudes as a task that troubled them, we see that the utmost benevolence, through which one embodies Heaven and Earth, cannot cease. Why is this? In bringing forth living things, Heaven and Earth preside knowingly over the great beginning and act to bring things to completion. Their blowing becomes wind, their breath becomes mist; their anger brings bleakness, their joy brings ease. They stir things with thunder, moisten them with rain and dew, and give them rest through the alternation of day and night, exerting their powers to the utmost in every respect. Thus, in their relation to the myriad things, Heaven and Earth seem to have something in their hearts that permits no relaxation. This indeed is their utmost benevolence, and the sage, fully realizing his bodily form, faithfully resembles them. Hence he is impartial like Heaven and Earth, and his utmost benevolence ranks alongside theirs. He therefore regards as his body not merely his own individual person, but the vast, inexhaustible expanse of Heaven and Earth. He does not seek the convenience of his own comfort, but constantly attends to whether all things have found their proper place.
Ah! How encompassing is the love in the sage’s heart, and how great its capacity! In relation to all under Heaven, the sage truly has things that his heart cannot bear. Now, when someone handles a precious vessel, even after placing it on suitable ground, he still cushions it with rushes. Why? His love for the vessel prompts this care. How much more must this apply to his own body! He nurtures and sustains it to prolong the wellspring of its life, feeds it with fine grain and meat to nourish its vitality, and uses medicines and medicinal stones to dispel its illnesses. Adapting his care to the seasons and circumstances, he makes every provision for its nourishment, within and without. Thus, if his finger is unlike other people’s, he seeks to straighten it, considering even Qin or Chu no great distance to travel, because it belongs to his own body. If his hands and feet are withered and numb, yet his heart remains unaware of them, then…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
不仁之甚者矣而非所以言愛身也愛身者無
所擇于其身則愛天下者寧有所擇于天下哉
今夫天地之間物類至繁動而爲鳥獸植而爲
草木靈而爲人有君臣父子夫婦長幼朋友之
倫焉有喜怒哀樂居處飽煖之情焉有疲癃殘
疾顛連無告之戚焉其衝撞叫號羣居雜處交
願類首而俯仰于兩間者若是其弗齊焉聖人
者以其所不忍之心發而爲不忍之政其視萬
物固吾之四體百骸也故培持涵養遂吾生也
===
則取之以時用之以度以遂其生修身履道盡
吾倫也則經之綸之品之節之以盡其倫備物
致用以順吾情也則爲約束誓戒屋宇衣服以
各順其情周恤保愛以去吾身之疾痛疴癢也
則使天下有所歸有所養置諸袵席之上而運
人至仁之心始已其所以處已也即所以處天
下也蓋不如是不足以盡仁而天地之所以爲
天地者冒萬有而不外者也而吾之所以無媿
于天地者謂能贊其化育也天地無間于萬物
punctuated: 不仁之甚者矣，而非所以言愛身也。愛身者無所擇于其身，則愛天下者寧有所擇于天下哉？今夫天地之間，物類至繁：動而爲鳥獸，植而爲草木，靈而爲人。有君臣、父子、夫婦、長幼、朋友之倫焉，有喜怒哀樂、居處飽煖之情焉，有疲癃殘疾、顛連無告之戚焉。其衝撞叫號，羣居雜處，交願類首而俯仰于兩間者，若是其弗齊焉。聖人者，以其所不忍之心，發而爲不忍之政。其視萬物，固吾之四體百骸也。故培持涵養，遂吾生也，則取之以時，用之以度，以遂其生；修身履道，盡吾倫也，則經之綸之，品之節之，以盡其倫；備物致用，以順吾情也，則爲約束誓戒、屋宇衣服，以各順其情；周恤保愛，以去吾身之疾痛疴癢也，則使天下有所歸，有所養，置諸袵席之上，而運人至仁之心始已。其所以處已也，即所以處天下也。蓋不如是不足以盡仁，而天地之所以爲天地者，冒萬有而不外者也。而吾之所以無媿于天地者，謂能贊其化育也。天地無間于萬物
translation_en:
…this is insensibility in the extreme, and cannot be called caring for one’s own body. If those who care for their bodies make no distinctions among their parts, could those who care for all under Heaven make distinctions within it? Between Heaven and Earth, the kinds of beings are exceedingly numerous: those that move are birds and beasts; those that grow rooted are plants and trees; those endowed with spiritual intelligence are human beings. There are the relationships between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friend and friend. There are the feelings of joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, and the needs for shelter, sufficient food, and warmth. There are the afflictions of exhaustion, infirmity, and disability, of distress and helplessness with no one to appeal to. They jostle and cry out, dwell in groups and mingle together, their wishes intersecting and their heads gathered by kind [?], looking down and up between Heaven and Earth: such is their diversity.

The sage gives expression to his heart that cannot bear others’ suffering through government that cannot bear their suffering. He regards the myriad beings as his own limbs and bones. Thus, just as nurturing and sustaining himself allows his own life to flourish, he takes from other beings at the proper seasons and uses them within due limits, allowing their lives to flourish. Just as cultivating himself and following the Way fulfills his own human relationships, he orders and arranges theirs, distinguishing their ranks and regulating them, so that they may fulfill their relationships. Just as providing things and putting them to use satisfies his own needs, he establishes rules, pledges, and admonitions, and provides houses and clothing, so that each may have their needs satisfied. Just as relief, protection, and loving care remove illness, pain, and irritation from his own body, he ensures that all under Heaven have somewhere to turn and means of support, settling them upon bedding and mats; only then does his exercise of the heart of utmost benevolence cease [?]. The way he treats himself is precisely the way he treats all under Heaven.

Unless he acts thus, he cannot fully realize benevolence. What makes Heaven and Earth Heaven and Earth is that they encompass all existence and exclude nothing. What enables us to stand without shame before Heaven and Earth is our capacity to assist their transforming and nourishing activity. Heaven and Earth admit no separation between themselves and the myriad beings…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
而吾少有間于天地則謂之不肖謂之棄人嗚
呼天地之仁無棄物也而聖人之仁寧有棄人
哉故造化不雕刻而人物阜至仁不矯强而位
育致天地以兩儀範之而不見其有餘聖人以
一心運之而不見其不足故曰天施地生非聖
人不成天覆地承非聖人不明天神地容非聖
人而誰爲貞則聖人之于天地誠不可以形骸
擬也是故三皇繼天而道無爲五帝立極而功
難言三王體仁而天下化伊周以仁相天下孔
===
孟以仁師天下葢誠有見天地之即吾身而分
量不容于一私小之也是故天地惟不貳也而
莫測其生物之功聖人惟不息也而漸著其悠
久之用天地之化聖人之心一誠之運也吾獨
悲世之談天地者歸諸眇茫之末而不本其生
物之功而言仁者舉其煦煦之節而不究其本
體之全不病于無愛則病于爲我使聖人與天
地若不相似然而不知純亦不已聖人葢亦天
地矣然則有志于是者奚始亦曰能近取譬而
punctuated: 而吾少有間于天地，則謂之不肖，謂之棄人。嗚呼！天地之仁無棄物也，而聖人之仁寧有棄人哉？故造化不雕刻而人物阜，至仁不矯强而位育致。天地以兩儀範之，而不見其有餘；聖人以一心運之，而不見其不足。故曰：「天施地生，非聖人不成；天覆地承，非聖人不明；天神地容，非聖人而誰爲貞？」則聖人之于天地，誠不可以形骸擬也。是故三皇繼天而道無爲，五帝立極而功難言，三王體仁而天下化，伊周以仁相天下，孔孟以仁師天下。葢誠有見天地之即吾身，而分量不容于一私小之也。是故天地惟不貳也，而莫測其生物之功；聖人惟不息也，而漸著其悠久之用。天地之化，聖人之心，一誠之運也。吾獨悲世之談天地者，歸諸眇茫之末，而不本其生物之功；而言仁者，舉其煦煦之節，而不究其本體之全。不病于無愛，則病于爲我，使聖人與天地若不相似然，而不知純亦不已，聖人葢亦天地矣。然則有志于是者奚始？亦曰能近取譬而
translation_en:
…yet if I depart even slightly from Heaven and Earth, I am called unworthy, a person cast aside. Alas! The benevolence of Heaven and Earth casts aside no thing; could the benevolence of the sage cast aside any person? Thus, without carving or shaping, the creative processes bring people and things to abundance; without forced effort, perfect benevolence brings Heaven and Earth to their proper positions and the myriad things to full nurture. Heaven and Earth give this form through the two cosmic powers, without appearing to have any surplus; the sage sets it in motion through a single mind, without appearing to have any deficiency. Hence it is said: “Heaven bestows and Earth gives birth; without the sage, their work is not completed. Heaven covers and Earth supports; without the sage, their work is not made manifest. Heaven is numinous and Earth accommodating; who but the sage can establish their right order?” Truly, then, the sage’s relation to Heaven and Earth cannot be assessed by comparing their physical forms.

Thus the Three Sovereigns succeeded Heaven, and their Way was without deliberate action; the Five Emperors established the supreme standard, and their achievements defy description; the Three Kings embodied benevolence, and all under Heaven were transformed. Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou assisted in governing all under Heaven through benevolence; Kongzi and Mengzi taught all under Heaven through benevolence. They truly perceived that Heaven and Earth were their own selves, and that this capacity could not be diminished by a single selfish thought. It is precisely because Heaven and Earth are undivided that their achievement in generating things is unfathomable; precisely because the sage never ceases that the enduring efficacy of his work gradually becomes manifest. The transformations of Heaven and Earth and the mind of the sage are the operation of one sincerity.

I lament that those in this age who discuss Heaven and Earth consign them to obscure and remote trivialities, rather than grounding their account in their work of generating things; and that those who speak of benevolence cite its little acts of kindness without investigating the completeness of its fundamental substance. They suffer either from a lack of love or from selfishness, making the sage appear unlike Heaven and Earth. They do not understand the saying, “Pure, and likewise unceasing”: the sage, indeed, is also Heaven and Earth. Where, then, should someone aspiring to this begin? Simply with the ability to draw analogies from what is close at hand…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
已蓋一命之士苟存心于利物亦足有濟則存
者所以存此誠也由怵惕孺子之初之誠而充
之以造乎其極則仁可至而天地可幾至于聖
人之所不能者吾亦安之而已否則不得其方
非子貢之過求則宰我之過慮耳又奚足以知
聖人之心而識所謂至仁者哉
同前
張洲
同考試官教諭何　批〔天地一身之理發明殆盡敬服〕
===
考試官學正蔡　批〔意有餘而不貴辭可式〕
考試官學正周　批〔純全天德之言〕
聖人之心無我而其視萬物也無非我夫物我
分於有身其形睽仁愛生於本心其理合苟就
夫睽之者言之也則亦曰吾愛吾身吾足矣而於
人且物也何有其人且物之各有身吾又能安
能一而愛之也此不足以成身者也而害仁甚
矣仁之爲文從人從二人其人者謂之仁故有
我非也不以物爲我者亦非也聖人仁之至者
punctuated:
已。蓋一命之士，苟存心于利物，亦足有濟，則存者所以存此誠也。由怵惕孺子之初之誠，而充之以造乎其極，則仁可至，而天地可幾。至于聖人之所不能者，吾亦安之而已。否則不得其方，非子貢之過求，則宰我之過慮耳。又奚足以知聖人之心，而識所謂至仁者哉？
同前。
張洲。
同考試官教諭何，批〔天地一身之理，發明殆盡，敬服。〕
考試官學正蔡，批〔意有餘而不貴辭，可式。〕
考試官學正周，批〔純全天德之言。〕
聖人之心無我，而其視萬物也，無非我。夫物我分於有身，其形睽；仁愛生於本心，其理合。苟就夫睽之者言之也，則亦曰：「吾愛吾身，吾足矣，而於人且物也何有？其人且物之各有身，吾又能安能一而愛之也？」此不足以成身者也，而害仁甚矣。仁之爲文，從人從二，人其人者謂之仁。故有我非也，不以物爲我者亦非也。聖人，仁之至者
translation_en:
…that is all. Even an officer of the lowest rank, if he keeps his mind intent on benefiting others, can accomplish some good. What he preserves in his mind is precisely this sincerity. Beginning with the sincerity of the first alarm felt at a child’s peril, he extends it to its utmost reach; then benevolence can be attained, and Heaven and Earth approached. As for what even the sage cannot accomplish, I too simply accept it. Otherwise, one fails to find the proper method: one either demands too much, like Zigong, or worries too much, like Zai Wo. How could this suffice to understand the sage’s mind and recognize what is called perfect benevolence?
Same topic as above.
Zhang Zhou.
Associate Examiner He, an Instructor, comments: 〔The principle that Heaven and Earth form one body is elucidated almost exhaustively. I am respectfully impressed.〕
Examiner Cai, a School Director, comments: 〔Rich in meaning without prizing ornate language; it can serve as a model.〕
Examiner Zhou, a School Director, comments: 〔Words expressing the pure wholeness of Heaven’s virtue.〕
The sage’s mind is without self, yet when he regards the myriad things, none is outside his self. Other things and oneself are separated by having bodies: their physical forms are distinct. Benevolent love arises from the original mind: in principle they are united. If one speaks only of their distinctness, one merely says: “I love my own body, and that suffices for me. What concern have I for other people and things? Since those people and things each have bodies of their own, how could I possibly unite them and love them all?” [?] This is insufficient to bring one’s own person to fulfillment, and it gravely harms benevolence. The written character for benevolence, ren 仁, combines “person” 人 and “two” 二. To treat other people as people is called benevolence. Thus, having a separate self is wrong; failing to regard other things as oneself is also wrong. The sage is one in whom benevolence reaches its utmost…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
也豈肯有我以自畀薄其身是必兼萬物而我
之合天下以成其身而後聖人之心始慰聖人
之身大矣哉聖人之身何身也天地之身也天
與地爲身是故日月星辰繫之雨風露雷化之
寒暑經緯之山川草木奠麗之禽獸夷狄雜著
之猶曰其耳目口鼻毛髮骨血吹噓喜怒以至
四肢百骸之不可一缺焉者觀天地於人質而
當近而不誣以其中之所具者名之爲一身其
誰曰不然而在於人耳目口鼻毛髮骨血吹噓
===
喜怒四肢百骸非可相待而有者也謂聖人以
衆人爲一身迂而曲判而不屬人則疑矣况乎
曰日月星辰雨風露雷寒暑山川草木禽獸夷
狄皆曰聖人之身之所有也支而誕蕩而不情
誰其不駭聞乎曰形不同而理同聖人不以形
廢理也事不同而道同聖人必以道體事也衆
人有見於身無見於天地故不以天下之愛易
其身聖人見天地之身卽其身也故以其所愛
身者通天下若曰天地之有是衆形也欲其並
punctuated: 也，豈肯有我以自畀薄其身？是必兼萬物而我之，合天下以成其身，而後聖人之心始慰。聖人之身大矣哉！聖人之身何身也？天地之身也。天與地爲身，是故日月星辰繫之，雨風露雷化之，寒暑經緯之，山川草木奠麗之，禽獸夷狄雜著之，猶曰其耳目口鼻、毛髮骨血、吹噓喜怒，以至四肢百骸之不可一缺焉者。觀天地於人，質而當，近而不誣，以其中之所具者名之爲一身，其誰曰不然？而在於人，耳目口鼻、毛髮骨血、吹噓喜怒、四肢百骸，非可相待而有者也。謂聖人以衆人爲一身，迂而曲，判而不屬，人則疑矣。况乎曰日月星辰、雨風露雷、寒暑、山川草木、禽獸夷狄，皆曰聖人之身之所有也，支而誕，蕩而不情，誰其不駭聞乎？曰：形不同而理同，聖人不以形廢理也；事不同而道同，聖人必以道體事也。衆人有見於身，無見於天地，故不以天下之愛易其身。聖人見天地之身卽其身也，故以其所愛身者通天下。若曰天地之有是衆形也，欲其並
translation_en:
…how could he consent to have a private self, thereby diminishing his own person [?]? He must embrace the myriad things and regard them as himself, uniting all under Heaven to constitute his own person; only then is the sage’s heart satisfied. How vast is the sage’s person! What sort of body is it? It is the body of Heaven and Earth. With Heaven and Earth as his body, the sun, moon, and stars are attached to it; rain, wind, dew, and thunder transform it; cold and heat run through it like warp and weft; mountains, rivers, plants, and trees stand firmly within it; birds, beasts, and the Yi and Di peoples appear intermingled within it. These are like his ears, eyes, mouth, nose, hair, bones, blood, breathing, joy, and anger, down to his four limbs and hundred bodily parts: not one can be missing. To view Heaven and Earth in terms of a human being is concrete and fitting, familiar and free of falsehood. To call all that they contain a single body—who would deny that this is so? Yet in human beings, ears, eyes, mouth, nose, hair, bones, blood, breathing, joy, anger, the four limbs, and the hundred bodily parts cannot exist through mutual dependence [?]. To say that the sage regards all people as one body seems far-fetched and tortuous, disconnected and unrelated; people therefore doubt it. How much more so when one says that the sun, moon, and stars, rain, wind, dew, and thunder, cold and heat, mountains, rivers, plants, trees, birds, beasts, and the Yi and Di peoples all belong to the sage’s own body! This seems rambling and extravagant, unrestrained and contrary to reality. Who would not be startled to hear it?

The reply is: their forms differ, but their principle is the same; the sage does not discard principle on account of form. Affairs differ, but the Way is the same; the sage invariably uses the Way to embody affairs. Ordinary people perceive their own persons but do not perceive Heaven and Earth; thus they will not exchange concern for their own persons for love of all under Heaven. The sage sees the body of Heaven and Earth as his own body, and therefore extends throughout all under Heaven the love he bears for his own person. It is as though he were saying: Heaven and Earth possess these many forms and desire that they together…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
育並行者其心也而至以萬物爲芻狗人猶得
而病其不仁少有災祥寒暑未宜人且將以爲
憾矣吾人者得天地之心以爲心者也固天所
以使之裁成輔相儕力斯仁者也故舉天地之
化育皆吾之所當有事而其病且憾者吾亦與
有責焉耳是故不敢私其身於我而必通其身
於天地也禹思天下有溺者猶已溺之稷思天
下有饑者猶已饑之猶曰任其職云爾至於伊
尹耕莘之夫乃思天下匹夫匹婦有不與被堯
===
舜之澤者若已推而納之溝中茍無見於一身
之義則其狂也聖人何取乎是故私其身於我
者自小其身者也指不若人不遠秦楚以求伸
尺寸之膚無不愛且養也而戕物以利其身者
將必爲之即有此身何取於此身乎公其身於
天下者超乎有身之外者也天地不位以爲吾
大體之傷萬物不育以爲吾小體之顛瘁也而
致中致和之調劑自不能已茍成此身則參天
地之身也何其貴乎然小其身者未害也而勢
punctuated: 育並行者，其心也。而至以萬物爲芻狗，人猶得而病其不仁；少有災祥，寒暑未宜，人且將以爲憾矣。吾人者，得天地之心以爲心者也，固天所以使之裁成輔相、儕力斯仁者也。故舉天地之化育，皆吾之所當有事，而其病且憾者，吾亦與有責焉耳。是故不敢私其身於我，而必通其身於天地也。禹思天下有溺者，猶已溺之；稷思天下有饑者，猶已饑之，猶曰任其職云爾。至於伊尹，耕莘之夫，乃思天下匹夫匹婦有不與被堯舜之澤者，若已推而納之溝中。茍無見於一身之義，則其狂也，聖人何取乎？是故私其身於我者，自小其身者也。指不若人，不遠秦楚以求伸；尺寸之膚，無不愛且養也。而戕物以利其身者，將必爲之。即有此身，何取於此身乎？公其身於天下者，超乎有身之外者也。天地不位，以爲吾大體之傷；萬物不育，以爲吾小體之顛瘁也。而致中致和之調劑，自不能已。茍成此身，則參天地之身也，何其貴乎！然小其身者，未害也，而勢
translation_en:
…to grow together and proceed together: this is the heart of Heaven and Earth. Yet when they go so far as to treat the myriad things as straw dogs, people can still fault them for lacking benevolence. Should there be even minor calamities or portents, or cold and heat come out of season, people will moreover resent them. We humans take the heart of Heaven and Earth as our own heart. Indeed, Heaven thereby charges us to shape and assist its workings and to exert ourselves together in this benevolence. Thus the whole transforming and nurturing activity of Heaven and Earth is something in which we ought to engage; where people find fault or feel resentment, we too share responsibility. For this reason, we dare not reserve our person for ourselves alone, but must extend it into communion with Heaven and Earth.

Yu thought that if anyone under Heaven drowned, it was as though he himself had drowned that person; Ji thought that if anyone under Heaven went hungry, it was as though he himself had caused that hunger. One might still say that they were merely discharging their offices. But Yi Yin, a man who tilled the fields in Shen, thought that if any ordinary man or woman under Heaven failed to receive the beneficence of Yao and Shun, it was as though he himself had pushed them into a ditch. Had he possessed no insight into the meaning of forming one body, this would have been madness: what would the sages have found commendable in it?

Thus those who reserve their person for themselves alone diminish themselves. If a finger is unlike other people’s, they will think nothing of the distance to Qin or Chu to seek a way to straighten it; not an inch of their skin goes unloved or untended. Yet they will assuredly harm other beings to benefit themselves. Even if they possess this body, what is worthy of esteem in it? Those who make their person common to all under Heaven transcend the bounds of bodily existence. If Heaven and Earth are not in their proper places, they regard it as an injury to their greater body; if the myriad things do not flourish, they regard it as the affliction and exhaustion of their lesser body. They therefore cannot cease their efforts to bring things into balance by realizing equilibrium and harmony to the utmost. If they perfect this person, they stand as a third alongside Heaven and Earth, forming one body with them. How exalted this is! Yet merely diminishing oneself does no harm in itself; but the inevitable tendency…

title: 嘉靖二十五年山西鄉試錄
text:
必恣耳目口鼻之欲人之恣耳目口鼻之欲而
役其身者豈少哉故不仁者有其身未必不亡
大其身者必使無一物不得其所而後以爲吾
身之安此仰如天好生之仁者乃能使鳥獸草
木咸若之堯舜也雖謂之與天地長存可也故
至仁者外其身所以爲存嗚呼身一也爲我爲
物而公私判焉小大繫焉貴賤存亡關焉識仁
者可無辨哉聖人愛身之情與衆人同以其愛
身者而愛天下之凡有身故其仁博衆人愛身
===
之情亦與聖人同以其愛身者而厲天下之凡
有身故其心忍愛其身以及天下是謂身以天
下而品物萬形之不可解於心者無乎其弗賴
矣厲天下以愛其身是謂自棄其身卒之手足
痿痺且將不知也不仁孰甚焉是聖人之罪人
也曰爲我非矣無愛者仁乎曰楚人不問秦人
之肥瘠固無取於仁不愛其親而愛他人者君
子謂之悖德是故仁有量不可不充也仁有分
不可無辨也孟子曰親親而仁民仁民而愛物
punctuated:
必恣耳目口鼻之欲。人之恣耳目口鼻之欲而役其身者，豈少哉？故不仁者有其身，未必不亡。大其身者，必使無一物不得其所，而後以爲吾身之安。此仰如天好生之仁者，乃能使鳥獸草木咸若之堯舜也。雖謂之與天地長存，可也。故至仁者外其身，所以爲存。嗚呼！身一也，爲我爲物，而公私判焉，小大繫焉，貴賤存亡關焉。識仁者可無辨哉？聖人愛身之情與衆人同，以其愛身者而愛天下之凡有身，故其仁博。衆人愛身之情亦與聖人同，以其愛身者而厲天下之凡有身，故其心忍。愛其身以及天下，是謂身以天下，而品物萬形之不可解於心者，無乎其弗賴矣。厲天下以愛其身，是謂自棄其身。卒之手足痿痺，且將不知也。不仁孰甚焉？是聖人之罪人也。
曰：「爲我非矣，無愛者仁乎？」曰：「楚人不問秦人之肥瘠，固無取於仁。不愛其親而愛他人者，君子謂之悖德。是故仁有量，不可不充也；仁有分，不可無辨也。」孟子曰：「親親而仁民，仁民而愛物。」
translation_en:
…will inevitably indulge the desires of the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose. Are there few who indulge these desires and enslave their own persons? Thus those without benevolence, though they possess their persons, may nevertheless lose them. Those who enlarge their persons must ensure that nothing fails to find its proper place; only then do they consider their own persons at ease. Such benevolent men, looking upward and resembling Heaven in its love of life [?], are indeed Yao and Shun, who could bring birds, beasts, grasses, and trees alike into harmony. One may even say that they endure as long as Heaven and Earth. Thus those of consummate benevolence put their own persons outside their concern, and thereby preserve them. Alas!
